8	# Building with Rust
9	
10	Native Shell apps are written in Rust, in TSX, or in both. All three run on the same engine: the reactive graph, the
11	renderer, Taffy layout and the native modules (navigation, dialogs, the keyboard, the status bar) are Rust in every case, and every platform renders with its
12	own UI. What differs is the language of your own code, and with it whether the app carries a JavaScript VM.
13	
14	| | Rust | TSX | Rust with TSX |
15	|---|---|---|---|
16	| Your UI, state and handlers | Rust | TSX on QuickJS | Rust components and modules, TSX screens that use them |
17	| The app runs | the engine and your crate only, on every platform and in the browser | QuickJS and the engine (in the browser, its JavaScript engine) | QuickJS and the engine, with your crate (in the browser, its JavaScript engine) |
18	| Suits | Medium and large apps with demanding business logic | Apps and modules delivered at run time, quick iteration | A Rust core with parts that change often |
19	| Edits | Rebuild and restart | Hot updates | Hot updates for TSX, rebuild and restart for Rust |
20	| Start | `nsh init my-app --template rust` | `nsh init my-app --template ts` | `nsh init my-app --template mixed` |
21	
22	## Choosing
23	
24	**Rust** suits apps whose business logic is large and demanding: trading, editors, data-heavy tools. You get Rust's
25	type system and compile-time checks across the whole app, the crates.io ecosystem, native performance for your own
26	code (not only for NSH's), and headless tests of the real UI with `cargo test`. The app is Rust and native code from
27	start to end: no JavaScript VM ships with it or runs in it, on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, GPUI and the web.
28	Components are functions that run once and bind signals to what they show, as in TSX ([Reactivity](./reactivity.md)),
29	written with typed styles instead of class strings.
30	
31	**TSX** suits UI that arrives after the app ships: modules a native app loads at run time, generated by a model or
32	written by another team, delivered as [signed packages](./signed-packages.md) and run in a sandbox the host configures,
33	with hot updates while you develop.
34	
35	**Rust with TSX** keeps the Rust core and adds TSX where it pays off: screens, settings, onboarding, experiments,
36	anything you iterate on with hot updates or deliver at run time as a [signed package](./signed-packages.md). TSX
37	imports your Rust components and modules like any NSH module, so the two halves meet at typed interfaces. The TSX
38	runs on QuickJS, which the app then carries.
39	
40	## An app written in Rust
41	
42	```sh
43	nsh init my-app --template rust
44	cd my-app
45	nsh run                        # this machine's backend; --target ios, android, web, macos, linux or windows
46	nsh package --target web       # or ios, ios-simulator, android, macos, linux, windows
47	```
48	
49	`src/lib.rs` holds the app: components, state, handlers, tasks.
50	
51	```rust
52	use nsh_base::{button, theme};
53	use nsh_core::prelude::*;
54	
55	/// The components available to TSX through `app/native`.
56	#[native_module("app/native")]
57	fn native(registry: &mut Registry) {
58	    registry.register::<App>();
59	}
60	
61	#[component]
62	pub fn App() -> impl IntoElement {
63	    let count = signal(0_u32);
64	    let quote = signal(SharedString::from("…"));
65	    // Async work runs in tasks; requests go through NSH's network stack.
66	    spawn(async move {
67	        if let Ok(response) = fetch("https://api.example.com/quote").await {
68	            quote.set(response.text().into());
69	        }
70	    });
71	    view()
72	        .flex_1()
73	        .items_center()
74	        .justify_center()
75	        .gap_4()
76	        .child(text(move || format!("Count: {}", count.get())))
77	        .child(text(quote))
78	        .child(
79	            // nsh_base's unstyled button, drawn with the theme's colors.
80	            button()
81	                .px(px(20.0))
82	                .py(px(12.0))
83	                .rounded(move || theme().radius)
84	                .bg(move || theme().primary)
85	                .active(|s| s.bg(move || theme().primary.opacity(0.9)))
86	                .on_press(move || count.update(|c| *c += 1))
87	                .child(text("Tap").text_color(move || theme().primary_foreground)),
88	        )
89	}
90	```
91	
92	Elements and components are made the same way: a function makes one (`view()`, `text(..)`, `nsh_base`'s
93	`button()`, your `#[component] fn Chart`'s `chart()`), and its methods set its props, one setter per prop (a value,
94	a signal or a closure), and its listeners, one method per event. Listeners are closures of their event
95	(`move |text: &str| ..`), and `move || ..` for an event without data; `.child(..)` takes an element, or an
96	`Option`, a `Vec`, an array or an iterator of elements (`.child(rows.iter().map(|r| row(r)))`).
97	
98	`nsh.json` names the root, and `nsh` mounts it:
99	
100	```json
101	{
102	  "name": "My App",
103	  "rust": ".",
104	  "root": "App",
105	  "theme": "theme.json",
106	  "appearance": "system"
107	}
108	```
109	
110	`"root"` is the component's path in the crate (`App`, `shell::Gallery`; in the first one with
111	[several crates](#several-crates)); `"theme"` is the [theme](#theme) its components draw with, and `"appearance"` applies to it as it does to a TSX app. With it,
112	`nsh run` and `nsh package` of the app's directory build the app's own runner for the target, with the root mounted
113	and no QuickJS linked in:
114	
115	| Target | What runs |
116	|---|---|
117	| macOS, Windows, Linux | The release runner with your crate, in a window; `nsh run` runs a debug build and shows the app's logs in the terminal |
118	| iOS, the iOS simulator, Mac Catalyst | The iOS runner with your crate, in an app |
119	| Android | The app's `libnsh.so` with your crate, started by the runtime's activity |
120	| Web | `nsh.wasm` with the engine and your crate (3.3 MB for the whole Rust gallery, 0.75 MB with brotli); the page mounts the root |
121	
122	`nsh` builds what your crate needs and nothing more: a small program of your crate and NSH's core that describes its
123	components and modules to the CLI, which then does the rest itself, and the runner of each target you run or
124	package. The first build of a new Rust app compiles your crate and NSH's core, about 60 crates. `nsh test` runs
125	the app's tests headless in a runner of your crate built the same way.
126	
127	On Linux, your crate selects optional platform features. Enable `webview` on your
128	`nsh-platform-linux` dependency to use web views; this links WebKitGTK 6.0, which must be installed to build and run
129	the app. The generated runner inherits that choice through Cargo feature unification.
130	
131	During `nsh run`, a change to the crate's Rust code builds the runner again and restarts the app; in the browser,
132	the open page loads the new runtime by itself. `cargo run` starts the same root directly on the desktop backend
133	(`src/main.rs`), and native apps that embed NSH mount a Rust root with `AppSource::Rust` on the `AppView` of macOS,
134	Windows, Linux, GPUI and iOS.
135	
136	Code for every platform, the web included, uses NSH's services: `fetch` for HTTP
137	([Networking](./networking.md#from-rust-components)), `timer`, `set_timeout` and `set_interval` for waiting,
138	`nsh_core::time::Instant` and `nsh_core::time::unix_ms()` for the clock. `background` and `blocking` run work on the
139	native targets' threads.

141	## Desktop title bars
142	
143	Rust apps draw their own title bars with `nsh_core::element::desktop`. Call
144	`set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Hidden, Some(height))`, mark the bar's background
145	with `.window_drag(true)`, and reserve the native window controls' space with
146	`title_bar()`. Its `top` is the bar's height, and `left` and `right` are the widths
147	occupied by the system controls. Reading it subscribes to changes, including full
148	screen. The platform handles window dragging and the user's title-bar double-click
149	behavior; `.window_drag(false)` keeps a child out of its parent's drag region.
150	
151	```rust
152	use nsh_core::{
153	    desktop::TitleBarStyle,
154	    element::{desktop::{close_window, set_title_bar, title_bar}}, prelude::*,
155	};
156	
157	fn window_bar() -> impl IntoElement {
158	    set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Hidden, Some(px(42.0)));
159	    view()
160	        .h(px(42.0))
161	        .flex_row()
162	        .items_center()
163	        .window_drag(true)
164	        .pl(move || title_bar().left + px(12.0))
165	        .pr(move || title_bar().right + px(12.0))
166	        .child(text("My app").flex_1())
167	        .child(text("Close").window_drag(false).on_press(close_window))
168	}
169	```
170	
171	`set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Default, None)` restores the system title bar.
172	`close_window()` follows the embedding host's normal window-close behavior.
173	The module has the window's other functions (`set_title`, `minimize`,
174	`toggle_full_screen`, ...) and the menus (`set_application_menu`,
175	`popup_menu`) too: [nsh/desktop](../modules/nsh-desktop.md).
176	
177	## Files and folders
178	
179	On the desktops, Rust code shows the system's file dialogs and hands local paths to
180	the system, each answer awaited in a task: `pick_paths` with an `OpenDialog`
181	(`OpenDialog::files()`, `::folders()` or `::files_and_folders()`), `pick_save_path`
182	with a `SaveDialog`, `open_path` (the file's default app), `reveal_path` (the item
183	selected in Finder, File Explorer or the file manager) and `move_to_trash` (where the
184	item went, when macOS says). The dialogs answer `Ok(None)` when the user cancels and
185	an error when they cannot show (on Linux without a file chooser portal, and on iOS,
186	Android and the web, where `open_path`, `reveal_path` and `move_to_trash` answer
187	an error too). Every request that fails answers its error, never `false`.
188	
189	```rust
190	use nsh_core::{
191	    file_dialog::{FileFilter, OpenDialog},
192	    prelude::*,
193	};
194	
195	fn open_notes() {
196	    let picked = pick_paths(
197	        OpenDialog::files()
198	            .multiple(true)
199	            .filter(FileFilter::new("Markdown", ["md", "markdown"]))
200	            .button_label("Open"),
201	    );
202	    spawn(async move {
203	        match picked.await {
204	            Ok(Some(paths)) => {
205	                for path in paths {
206	                    let _ = reveal_path(path).await;
207	                }
208	            }
209	            Ok(None) => {} // Cancelled.
210	            Err(error) => log::warn!("no file dialog: {error}"),
211	        }
212	    });
213	}
214	```

216	## Extending a Rust app with TSX
217	
218	The crate's `#[native_module("app/native")]` function names what TSX may import: components
219	(`registry.register::<Chart>()`), modules of functions (`registry.module::<Portfolio>()`, `#[module]` on a unit struct and its `impl`),
220	classes (`registry.class::<Ledger>()`, `#[class]` on a struct and its `impl`) and assets; the attribute also makes
221	`pub fn registry()` at the crate's root, the same set for your tests and other Rust code (`my_app_native::registry()`,
222	next to `nsh_base::registry()`). In a `#[module]` or
223	`#[class]` `impl`, the `pub fn`s are exported (`pub(crate)` too); functions without a visibility are helpers that
224	stay in Rust. Their TypeScript
225	declarations, doc comments included, are generated from the Rust types into `.nsh/types`, so TSX is checked against
226	them by `nsh check` and your editor:
227	
228	```rust
229	/// A price chart.
230	#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Props)]
231	pub struct ChartProps {
232	    /// The symbol to chart.
233	    pub symbol: Prop<SharedString>,
234	    /// The range shown.
235	    #[prop(default = SharedString::from("1D"))]
236	    pub range: Prop<SharedString>,
237	}
238	
239	#[derive(Event)]
240	pub enum ChartEvent {
241	    /// A price was selected.
242	    #[args(price)]
243	    Select(f64),
244	}
245	
246	/// A price chart; a press selects the last price.
247	#[component]
248	pub fn Chart(props: ChartProps, cx: Scope<ChartEvent>) -> impl IntoElement {
249	    view()
250	        .h(px(160.0))
251	        .bg(move || theme().muted)
252	        .on_press(move || cx.emit(ChartEvent::Select(101.5)))
253	        .child(text(move || format!("{} · {}", props.symbol.get(), props.range.get())))
254	}
255	
256	/// A ledger kept in Rust.
257	#[class]
258	pub struct Ledger {
259	    entries: Vec<f64>,
260	}
261	
262	#[class]
263	impl Ledger {
264	    /// An empty ledger.
265	    pub fn new() -> Self {
266	        Ledger { entries: Vec::new() }
267	    }
268	
269	    /// Adds `amount`; the new balance.
270	    pub fn add(&mut self, amount: f64) -> f64 {
271	        self.entries.push(amount);
272	        self.balance()
273	    }
274	
275	    /// The balance.
276	    #[getter]
277	    pub fn balance(&self) -> f64 {
278	        self.entries.iter().sum()
279	    }
280	
281	    /// Uploads the entries; resolves when the server has them.
282	    pub async fn upload(this: Instance<Ledger>, url: String) -> Result<(), String> {
283	        let body = this.with(|l| format!("{:?}", l.entries));
284	        fetch(HttpRequest::post(url, body)).await.map(|_| ())
285	    }
286	}
287	
288	/// The app's holdings.
289	#[module]
290	pub struct Portfolio;
291	
292	#[module]
293	impl Portfolio {
294	    /// The value of the holdings.
295	    pub fn total() -> f64 {
296	        1250.0
297	    }
298	}
299	```
300	
301	```tsx
302	import { mount, signal, View, Text } from "nsh";
303	import { Chart, Ledger, Portfolio } from "app/native";   // Rust
304	
305	const ledger = new Ledger();   // its state lives in Rust
306	
307	function Overview() {
308	  const balance = signal(ledger.add(Portfolio.total()));   // Rust, called at once
309	  return (
310	    <View class="gap-2 p-4">
311	      <Text>Balance: {balance()}</Text>
312	      <Chart symbol="NSH" range="1M" onSelect={(e) => balance.set(ledger.add(e.price))} />
313	      <View onPress={() => ledger.upload("https://example.com/ledger")} role="button" class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 active:bg-blue-700">
314	        <Text class="text-white">Upload</Text>
315	      </View>
316	    </View>
317	  );
318	}
319	
320	mount(() => <Overview />);
321	```
322	
323	Each export is documented in TypeScript by the doc comment of the Rust item that names it: a component by its
324	`#[component] fn` (`Chart`), a module and a class by their struct (`Portfolio`, `Ledger`), and props, events,
325	functions and members by their own (a setter needs none beside its getter). The `Props` struct's and the event
326	enum's own doc comments, and those of `impl` blocks, stay in Rust; a doc comment on a `#[module]` or `#[class]`
327	`impl` block is a compile error, since TypeScript would not show it. Each command that writes `.nsh/types` warns
328	about an export TSX sees without a doc comment, naming it (`Ledger.add`, `Chart.range`).
329	
330	TypeScript shows a doc comment up to its first heading. Notes for Rust callers, such as what `&self` borrows or
331	why a function takes `cx`, go under a heading, `# Rust` (or rustdoc's `# Panics`, `# Examples`), and stay in the
332	Rust docs:
333	
334	```rust
335	/// Puts `text` on the clipboard; resolves with the number of characters copied.
336	///
337	/// # Rust
338	///
339	/// Taking `cx` makes it an op, run in order with the UI changes TS made before it.
340	pub fn copy(text: String, cx: &mut ModuleCx) -> u32 {
341	    let count = text.chars().count() as u32;
342	    cx.set_clipboard(text);
343	    count
344	}
345	```
346	
347	Props are the fields of the component's `Props` struct and events the variants of its `Event` enum (`onSelect`),
348	both in camel case. Rust code places the same component with its constructor, a setter per prop and a listener
349	method per event: `chart().symbol("NSH").range("1M").on_select(move |price: &f64| last.set(*price))`. A Rust component's own content, events and state stay in Rust; TSX passes props in and hears
350	events. A prop of the wrong type (`level={1.5}` for a `u32` prop) is a warning, as on a built-in element: the
351	prop keeps its value and the rest of the component renders.
352	
353	A function or a member runs the way its Rust signature says. One that is not `async` runs inside the TSX call and
354	returns its value (`Portfolio.total()` is a number, `ledger.balance` a property): it computes and keeps state. An
355	`async fn` returns a Promise and runs as a task with NSH's services (`fetch`, `timer`, dialogs). A module function
356	taking `cx: &mut ModuleCx` reaches the platform in order with the UI (a toast, the status bar), and so does a
357	component's ref method; their return type decides what TSX gets: one returning `()` gives `void`, with no reply
358	(TSX calls it and moves on); one returning `Result<(), E>` gives `Promise<void>`, which rejects with the `Err`'s
359	message (the call runs with the UI's changes, after the TSX call returned, so the Promise carries its error; one
360	nobody awaits or catches is logged as an [unhandled rejection](./dev-server-and-debugging.md#logs)); one
361	returning a value gives `Promise<T>`. Arguments and results are typed from the signature: numbers, strings, `Option`, `Vec`, your
362	`#[derive(JsObject)]` structs and `#[derive(PropEnum)]` enums, instances of your classes, and TSX functions
363	(`Callback<A, R>`, which Rust calls at once inside a call, or later with `post` and `call_async`; TS sees
364	`(value: number) => void` for a `Callback<f64>`, and `#[args(balance)] listener: Callback<f64>` names the argument,
365	`(balance: number) => void`). A function that starts listening is named `on(event, listener)` and returns `Stop`
366	(`Stop::new(|| …)`), which TSX gets as a function that stops it (`() => void`); it runs once, when TSX calls it or
367	when what called `on` goes (a component, or the module's run under hot reload). An event's handler gets one object: a variant's value is its field `value`, which
368	`#[args(price)]` on the variant names (`onSelect({ price })`), and `#[args(open, reason)]` names the fields of a
369	variant of several. An argument of
370	the wrong type throws a `TypeError` in the call, or rejects the Promise of one that returns a Promise; an `Err`
371	throws (or rejects) with its message. A class's object owns its Rust value: it is freed when the object is collected, or at
372	once with `ledger.dispose()` (also `using ledger = new Ledger()`). Name the TSX entry to run it, `nsh run App.tsx` or `nsh package App.tsx --target …`: TSX edits are hot
373	updates, Rust edits rebuild and restart the app. The CLI bundles and compiles the TSX itself, knowing your crate's
374	exports from its description; the development hosts and `nsh test`'s headless runner are built with your crate and
375	QuickJS.
376	
377	`examples/rust-exports` in the repository is the reference for exporting: a small TSX app whose crate exports one
378	component (props required, defaulted and optional, an event, children), one module (a function of each kind) and
379	one class (a constructor, methods, a getter and a setter, a static, an `async` member, another instance as an
380	argument, a callback Rust posts to, `dispose()` and `using`), each with a short doc comment, and tests, in Rust and
381	in TypeScript (`App.test.tsx`), that press through the app and check what each one shows.
382	
383	`examples/gallery-rs` in the repository is a complete Rust app: every demo is Rust, `nsh run examples/gallery-rs
384	--target web` (or `ios`, `android`, …) runs its root, `nsh test examples/gallery-rs` runs its tests headless, and
385	`cargo run -p gallery-native` starts it on the desktop backend.
386	
387	### Render functions and the app's classes
388	
389	A component draws content of the app's for values it has (a row of its data, a code block of a document) with a
390	render function: a prop `Option<Renderer<T>>`, in TypeScript `(value: T) => JSX.Element`. The component calls
391	`render(key, value)` where the content goes and gets a view it styles and places as any other (inside a `text(..)`, an
392	inline view). The content is kept per key while the value stays equal, and rendered again when it changes. A Rust
393	parent passes a closure to the prop's setter (`quote().render_badge(|symbol| ..)`), which makes the
394	`Renderer` of it.
395	
396	Styles in a component are typed; the app's Tailwind classes reach one of its parts through a prop of classes and
397	`.app_class(..)` on that part's element. They apply after the element's own styles, with the app's theme, `dark:` and
398	the states, as `class` on an element does.
399	
400	```rust
401	/// A quote: its symbol, then content of the app's.
402	#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Props)]
403	pub struct QuoteProps {
404	    /// The symbol.
405	    pub symbol: Prop<SharedString>,
406	    /// Tailwind classes of the symbol's text.
407	    pub symbol_class: Prop<Option<SharedString>>,
408	    /// Content of the app's after the symbol (a change, a badge).
409	    pub render_badge: Prop<Option<Renderer<SharedString>>>,
410	}
411	
412	/// A quote of a symbol.
413	#[component]
414	pub fn Quote(props: QuoteProps) -> impl IntoElement {
415	    view()
416	        .flex_row()
417	        .items_center()
418	        .gap_2()
419	        .child(text(props.symbol).app_class(props.symbol_class))
420	        .child(dynamic(move || {
421	            props.render_badge.get().map(|r| r.render("badge", props.symbol.get()).flex_1())
422	        }))
423	}
424	```
425	
426	```tsx
427	<Quote
428	  symbol="NSH"
429	  symbolClass="text-lg font-semibold"
430	  renderBadge={(symbol) => <Text class="text-green-600">{`${symbol} ▲ 2.4%`}</Text>}
431	/>
432	```
433	
434	`TextView` in `nsh/base` is built this way: its `renderCodeBlock`, `renderMath`, ... are render functions, and its
435	`classes` are the app's classes by part ([TextView](../elements/text-view.md)).
436	
437	## Testing
438	
439	A Rust app's tests run it headless, in `cargo test` or in `nsh test`, with the same driver: on the real engine,
440	without a window, with display frames at 60 Hz, so timers, tasks and animations run as on screen. The driver starts
441	the app, keeps a model of the views it shows and takes steps (`press`, `type_text`, `submit`, `scroll`, `wait_for`)
442	on views named by selectors (a text, an accessibility label or a test id; `text:`, `label:`, `id:`); a step that
443	cannot be taken fails with the texts on screen.
444	
445	In `cargo test`, `nsh_testing::Headless` (nsh-testing's default features, without QuickJS) runs the root
446	(`app.screen()`: the texts on screen, the commands it sent); `EngineConfig::new` is a phone-sized engine with nothing
447	else set. `nsh test` runs TypeScript tests ([Testing](./testing-and-trace.md)) in a headless runner built with your
448	crates, where `open(".")` starts a Rust app's root:
449	
450	```toml
451	[dev-dependencies]
452	nsh-engine = "0.1"
453	nsh-testing = "0.1"
454	```
455	
456	```rust tabs
457	// tests/app.rs: cargo test
458	use nsh_engine::{EngineConfig, Root};
459	use nsh_testing::Headless;
460	
461	#[test]
462	fn a_tap_counts() {
463	    let mut app = Headless::start(EngineConfig::new(Root::of::<my_app::App>())).unwrap();
464	    app.wait_for("Count: 0").unwrap();
465	    app.press("Tap").unwrap();
466	    app.wait_for("Count: 1").unwrap();
467	}
468	```
469	
470	```tsx tabs
471	// App.test.tsx, next to nsh.json: nsh test
472	import { expect, open, test } from "nsh/test";
473	
474	test("a tap counts", async () => {
475	  const app = await open(".");
476	  await app.press("Tap");
477	  expect(app.texts()).toContain("Count: 1");
478	});
479	```
480	
481	A TSX entry is built with `nsh-testing`'s feature `bundle` as `nsh run` builds it, against the UI sets its hosts
482	serve: NSH's, and each crate's `registry()`, which `#[native_module]` makes:
483	
484	```toml
485	[dev-dependencies]
486	nsh-testing = { version = "0.1", features = ["bundle"] }
487	nsh-base = "0.1"
488	```
489	
490	```rust
491	#[test]
492	fn the_module_formats_money() {
493	    let sets = vec![nsh_base::registry(), my_app_native::registry()];
494	    let mut app = nsh_testing::tsx("../App.tsx", sets).unwrap();
495	    app.wait_for("Formatted at once: $1,234.50").unwrap();
496	}
497	```
498	
499	`nsh_testing::compile_tsx` builds the entry once for several tests, and `nsh_testing::start` hands the
500	batches to a test that keeps its own model of the screen. `examples/rust-exports` tests its TSX entry this way;
501	`examples/gallery-rs` tests its Rust root in TypeScript, a test file for about each demo.
502	
503	## Theme
504	
505	The look of an app is the app's own: NSH provides the primitives and the unstyled base components of `nsh_base`, and
506	your crate is the styled layer on top, the app's own component library ([Three layers](./architecture.md#three-layers)). Rust components take their colors, corner radius and fonts from a theme, `theme()` from
507	`nsh_base`, so one file restyles every component of the app. Each color has a light and a dark value;
508	when the system switches appearance, a binding such as `.bg(move || theme().primary)` changes color natively, with no
509	render.
510	
511	The theme has the design tokens of [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/theming), and its default is shadcn's
512	`neutral` theme, a black-and-white palette with a 10 pt corner radius. To use your own, set `"theme"` in `nsh.json`
513	to the path of a theme file, relative to `nsh.json`, or to the theme's content inline:
514	
515	```json
516	{
517	  "name": "My App",
518	  "rust": ".",
519	  "theme": "brand-theme.json"
520	}
521	```
522	
523	A theme file is shadcn's `cssVars`, the format of shadcn's themes and registry items, so a theme exported from
524	[shadcn's themes](https://ui.shadcn.com/themes) or [tweakcn](https://tweakcn.com) works as it is. `light` sets the
525	values of the light appearance, `dark` those of the dark one, and `theme` those of both:
526	
527	```json
528	{
529	  "cssVars": {
530	    "theme": {
531	      "radius": "0.5rem",
532	      "font-sans": "Inter, sans-serif"
533	    },
534	    "light": {
535	      "primary": "oklch(0.541 0.281 293.009)",
536	      "primary-foreground": "oklch(0.969 0.016 293.756)",
537	      "ring": "var(--primary)",
538	      "up": "#16a34a"
539	    },
540	    "dark": {
541	      "primary": "oklch(0.702 0.183 293.541)",
542	      "primary-foreground": "oklch(0.283 0.141 291.089)",
543	      "up": "#4ade80"
544	    }
545	  }
546	}
547	```
548	
549	- Your theme is applied over the default theme, so you list only what you change. A value `light` sets and `dark`
550	  leaves out is used in both appearances.
551	- Values are written as in CSS. Colors are any CSS color (`#7c3aed`, `rgb(…)`, `hsl(…)`, `oklch(…)`, `white`),
552	  `color-mix(in oklab, var(--primary) 80%, white)`, or another token of the same appearance, `var(--primary)` (with a
553	  fallback: `var(--brand, #7c3aed)`). Lengths are `rem` (16 points) or `px` (points). Fonts are font family lists:
554	  the first family that is not a generic one is used, and a generic first family (`system-ui`, `sans-serif`) is the
555	  system font.
556	- **Your own tokens.** Any other name is a token of the app, as a variable in Tailwind's `@theme` is: `"up"` above is
557	  `theme().color("up")` in Rust, `bg-up` / `text-up/70` in classes and `token("up")` in TSX
558	  ([Theme tokens](./tailwind.md#theme-tokens)). A number such as `"radius-card": "14px"` is `theme().number("radius-card")`
559	  and `rounded-(--radius-card)`.
560	- The bundler checks the theme when it builds: a missing file, invalid JSON or a theme other than `cssVars` fails the
561	  build with an `nsh.json: theme: …` error.
562	
563	The tokens, with their default light and dark values (shadcn's `neutral`):
564	
565	| Token | `theme()` | Light | Dark | Role |
566	|---|---|---|---|---|
567	| `background` / `foreground` | `background` / `foreground` | `oklch(1 0 0)` / `oklch(0.145 0 0)` | `oklch(0.145 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | The app's background, and the text on it |
568	| `card` / `card-foreground` | `card` / `card_foreground` | `oklch(1 0 0)` / `oklch(0.145 0 0)` | `oklch(0.205 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | Cards and grouped surfaces, and the text on them |
569	| `popover` / `popover-foreground` | `popover` / `popover_foreground` | `oklch(1 0 0)` / `oklch(0.145 0 0)` | `oklch(0.205 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | Popovers, menus and tooltips, and the text on them |
570	| `primary` / `primary-foreground` | `primary` / `primary_foreground` | `oklch(0.205 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | `oklch(0.922 0 0)` / `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | The main action (a primary button), and the text on it |
571	| `secondary` / `secondary-foreground` | `secondary` / `secondary_foreground` | `oklch(0.97 0 0)` / `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | `oklch(0.269 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | Secondary actions, and the text on them |
572	| `muted` / `muted-foreground` | `muted` / `muted_foreground` | `oklch(0.97 0 0)` / `oklch(0.556 0 0)` | `oklch(0.269 0 0)` / `oklch(0.708 0 0)` | Quiet surfaces; secondary text: captions, labels, placeholders |
573	| `accent` / `accent-foreground` | `accent` / `accent_foreground` | `oklch(0.97 0 0)` / `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | `oklch(0.269 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | A hovered or highlighted item, such as a menu item or list row, and its text |
574	| `destructive` | `destructive` | `oklch(0.577 0.245 27.325)` | `oklch(0.704 0.191 22.216)` | Destructive actions and errors |
575	| `border` | `border` | `oklch(0.922 0 0)` | `oklch(1 0 0 / 10%)` | Dividers and borders |
576	| `input` | `input` | `oklch(0.922 0 0)` | `oklch(1 0 0 / 15%)` | The border of inputs |
577	| `ring` | `ring` | `oklch(0.708 0 0)` | `oklch(0.556 0 0)` | Focus rings |
578	| `chart-1` … `chart-5` | `chart_1` … `chart_5` | `oklch(0.87 0 0)` … `oklch(0.269 0 0)` | the same | The series of a chart |
579	| `sidebar`, `sidebar-foreground`, `sidebar-primary`, `sidebar-primary-foreground`, `sidebar-accent`, `sidebar-accent-foreground`, `sidebar-border`, `sidebar-ring` | `sidebar`, `sidebar_foreground`, ... | `sidebar` `oklch(0.985 0 0)`, `sidebar-primary` `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | `sidebar` `oklch(0.205 0 0)`, `sidebar-primary` `oklch(0.488 0.243 264.376)` | A sidebar's surface, its main action, its highlighted item, borders and focus ring |
580	| `radius` | `radius` | `0.625rem` (10 pt) | | The corner radius |
581	| `font-sans` | `font_sans` | the system font | | The app's font: every text that sets no family of its own |
582	| `font-mono` | `font_mono` | the system monospace font | | The monospaced font: `font-mono`, code in `TextView` |
583	
584	## Several crates
585	
586	An app's Rust code can be split into crates, each imported by its own specifier: `"rust"` takes a list of crate
587	paths, and each crate in it has its own `#[native_module]` function.
588	
589	```json
590	{
591	  "rust": ["native/charts", "native/storage"],
592	  "root": "App"
593	}
594	```
595	
596	```tsx
597	import { Chart } from "app/charts";        // native/charts: #[native_module("app/charts")]
598	import { Store } from "app/storage";       // native/storage: #[native_module("app/storage")]
599	```
600	
601	Every runner and host links all of them, and `.nsh/types` declares each specifier. Crates share code through Cargo
602	path dependencies (`shared = { path = "../shared" }`): a crate of company components can be used by several crates
603	and listed by several apps, and only the crates listed in `"rust"` export to TSX. Each listed crate has a package
604	name and a specifier of its own; `nsh` reports a repeated one with the two paths that share it. A Rust app's
605	`"root"` is a component of the first crate listed. During `nsh run` and `nsh dev`, a change to any of them, or to a
606	crate they depend on by path, rebuilds the app and restarts it.
607	
608	## Browser APIs on the web
609	
610	On the web, a crate can call the browser's APIs (a WebSocket, `IndexedDB`, …) through wasm-bindgen and `web-sys`;
611	`nsh` builds the glue they need with the runtime. See [Web](./web.md#browser-apis-from-rust).
612	
613	## See also
614	
615	- [Project structure](./project-structure.md): every key of `nsh.json`.
616	- [Web](./web.md#apps-with-rust-components): Rust apps in the browser.
617	- [Networking](./networking.md#from-rust-components): `fetch` from Rust.
618	- [CLI](./cli.md#nsh-init): `nsh init --template rust` and `--template mixed`.

---
title: Building with Rust
description: "Write a Native Shell app entirely in Rust, with no QuickJS on any platform, or in Rust with TSX screens on top: when to choose which, and how the two share components and modules."
order: 5.5
group: start
---

# Building with Rust

Native Shell apps are written in Rust, in TSX, or in both. All three run on the same engine: the reactive graph, the
renderer, Taffy layout and the native modules (navigation, dialogs, the keyboard, the status bar) are Rust in every case, and every platform renders with its
own UI. What differs is the language of your own code, and with it whether the app carries a JavaScript VM.

| | Rust | TSX | Rust with TSX |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your UI, state and handlers | Rust | TSX on QuickJS | Rust components and modules, TSX screens that use them |
| The app runs | the engine and your crate only, on every platform and in the browser | QuickJS and the engine (in the browser, its JavaScript engine) | QuickJS and the engine, with your crate (in the browser, its JavaScript engine) |
| Suits | Medium and large apps with demanding business logic | Apps and modules delivered at run time, quick iteration | A Rust core with parts that change often |
| Edits | Rebuild and restart | Hot updates | Hot updates for TSX, rebuild and restart for Rust |
| Start | `nsh init my-app --template rust` | `nsh init my-app --template ts` | `nsh init my-app --template mixed` |

## Choosing

**Rust** suits apps whose business logic is large and demanding: trading, editors, data-heavy tools. You get Rust's
type system and compile-time checks across the whole app, the crates.io ecosystem, native performance for your own
code (not only for NSH's), and headless tests of the real UI with `cargo test`. The app is Rust and native code from
start to end: no JavaScript VM ships with it or runs in it, on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, GPUI and the web.
Components are functions that run once and bind signals to what they show, as in TSX ([Reactivity](./reactivity.md)),
written with typed styles instead of class strings.

**TSX** suits UI that arrives after the app ships: modules a native app loads at run time, generated by a model or
written by another team, delivered as [signed packages](./signed-packages.md) and run in a sandbox the host configures,
with hot updates while you develop.

**Rust with TSX** keeps the Rust core and adds TSX where it pays off: screens, settings, onboarding, experiments,
anything you iterate on with hot updates or deliver at run time as a [signed package](./signed-packages.md). TSX
imports your Rust components and modules like any NSH module, so the two halves meet at typed interfaces. The TSX
runs on QuickJS, which the app then carries.

## An app written in Rust

```sh
nsh init my-app --template rust
cd my-app
nsh run                        # this machine's backend; --target ios, android, web, macos, linux or windows
nsh package --target web       # or ios, ios-simulator, android, macos, linux, windows
```

`src/lib.rs` holds the app: components, state, handlers, tasks.

```rust
use nsh_base::{button, theme};
use nsh_core::prelude::*;

/// The components available to TSX through `app/native`.
#[native_module("app/native")]
fn native(registry: &mut Registry) {
    registry.register::<App>();
}

#[component]
pub fn App() -> impl IntoElement {
    let count = signal(0_u32);
    let quote = signal(SharedString::from("…"));
    // Async work runs in tasks; requests go through NSH's network stack.
    spawn(async move {
        if let Ok(response) = fetch("https://api.example.com/quote").await {
            quote.set(response.text().into());
        }
    });
    view()
        .flex_1()
        .items_center()
        .justify_center()
        .gap_4()
        .child(text(move || format!("Count: {}", count.get())))
        .child(text(quote))
        .child(
            // nsh_base's unstyled button, drawn with the theme's colors.
            button()
                .px(px(20.0))
                .py(px(12.0))
                .rounded(move || theme().radius)
                .bg(move || theme().primary)
                .active(|s| s.bg(move || theme().primary.opacity(0.9)))
                .on_press(move || count.update(|c| *c += 1))
                .child(text("Tap").text_color(move || theme().primary_foreground)),
        )
}
```

Elements and components are made the same way: a function makes one (`view()`, `text(..)`, `nsh_base`'s
`button()`, your `#[component] fn Chart`'s `chart()`), and its methods set its props, one setter per prop (a value,
a signal or a closure), and its listeners, one method per event. Listeners are closures of their event
(`move |text: &str| ..`), and `move || ..` for an event without data; `.child(..)` takes an element, or an
`Option`, a `Vec`, an array or an iterator of elements (`.child(rows.iter().map(|r| row(r)))`).

`nsh.json` names the root, and `nsh` mounts it:

```json
{
  "name": "My App",
  "rust": ".",
  "root": "App",
  "theme": "theme.json",
  "appearance": "system"
}
```

`"root"` is the component's path in the crate (`App`, `shell::Gallery`; in the first one with
[several crates](#several-crates)); `"theme"` is the [theme](#theme) its components draw with, and `"appearance"` applies to it as it does to a TSX app. With it,
`nsh run` and `nsh package` of the app's directory build the app's own runner for the target, with the root mounted
and no QuickJS linked in:

| Target | What runs |
|---|---|
| macOS, Windows, Linux | The release runner with your crate, in a window; `nsh run` runs a debug build and shows the app's logs in the terminal |
| iOS, the iOS simulator, Mac Catalyst | The iOS runner with your crate, in an app |
| Android | The app's `libnsh.so` with your crate, started by the runtime's activity |
| Web | `nsh.wasm` with the engine and your crate (3.3 MB for the whole Rust gallery, 0.75 MB with brotli); the page mounts the root |

`nsh` builds what your crate needs and nothing more: a small program of your crate and NSH's core that describes its
components and modules to the CLI, which then does the rest itself, and the runner of each target you run or
package. The first build of a new Rust app compiles your crate and NSH's core, about 60 crates. `nsh test` runs
the app's tests headless in a runner of your crate built the same way.

On Linux, your crate selects optional platform features. Enable `webview` on your
`nsh-platform-linux` dependency to use web views; this links WebKitGTK 6.0, which must be installed to build and run
the app. The generated runner inherits that choice through Cargo feature unification.

During `nsh run`, a change to the crate's Rust code builds the runner again and restarts the app; in the browser,
the open page loads the new runtime by itself. `cargo run` starts the same root directly on the desktop backend
(`src/main.rs`), and native apps that embed NSH mount a Rust root with `AppSource::Rust` on the `AppView` of macOS,
Windows, Linux, GPUI and iOS.

Code for every platform, the web included, uses NSH's services: `fetch` for HTTP
([Networking](./networking.md#from-rust-components)), `timer`, `set_timeout` and `set_interval` for waiting,
`nsh_core::time::Instant` and `nsh_core::time::unix_ms()` for the clock. `background` and `blocking` run work on the
native targets' threads.

## Desktop title bars

Rust apps draw their own title bars with `nsh_core::element::desktop`. Call
`set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Hidden, Some(height))`, mark the bar's background
with `.window_drag(true)`, and reserve the native window controls' space with
`title_bar()`. Its `top` is the bar's height, and `left` and `right` are the widths
occupied by the system controls. Reading it subscribes to changes, including full
screen. The platform handles window dragging and the user's title-bar double-click
behavior; `.window_drag(false)` keeps a child out of its parent's drag region.

```rust
use nsh_core::{
    desktop::TitleBarStyle,
    element::{desktop::{close_window, set_title_bar, title_bar}}, prelude::*,
};

fn window_bar() -> impl IntoElement {
    set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Hidden, Some(px(42.0)));
    view()
        .h(px(42.0))
        .flex_row()
        .items_center()
        .window_drag(true)
        .pl(move || title_bar().left + px(12.0))
        .pr(move || title_bar().right + px(12.0))
        .child(text("My app").flex_1())
        .child(text("Close").window_drag(false).on_press(close_window))
}
```

`set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Default, None)` restores the system title bar.
`close_window()` follows the embedding host's normal window-close behavior.
The module has the window's other functions (`set_title`, `minimize`,
`toggle_full_screen`, ...) and the menus (`set_application_menu`,
`popup_menu`) too: [nsh/desktop](../modules/nsh-desktop.md).

## Files and folders

On the desktops, Rust code shows the system's file dialogs and hands local paths to
the system, each answer awaited in a task: `pick_paths` with an `OpenDialog`
(`OpenDialog::files()`, `::folders()` or `::files_and_folders()`), `pick_save_path`
with a `SaveDialog`, `open_path` (the file's default app), `reveal_path` (the item
selected in Finder, File Explorer or the file manager) and `move_to_trash` (where the
item went, when macOS says). The dialogs answer `Ok(None)` when the user cancels and
an error when they cannot show (on Linux without a file chooser portal, and on iOS,
Android and the web, where `open_path`, `reveal_path` and `move_to_trash` answer
an error too). Every request that fails answers its error, never `false`.

```rust
use nsh_core::{
    file_dialog::{FileFilter, OpenDialog},
    prelude::*,
};

fn open_notes() {
    let picked = pick_paths(
        OpenDialog::files()
            .multiple(true)
            .filter(FileFilter::new("Markdown", ["md", "markdown"]))
            .button_label("Open"),
    );
    spawn(async move {
        match picked.await {
            Ok(Some(paths)) => {
                for path in paths {
                    let _ = reveal_path(path).await;
                }
            }
            Ok(None) => {} // Cancelled.
            Err(error) => log::warn!("no file dialog: {error}"),
        }
    });
}
```

## Extending a Rust app with TSX

The crate's `#[native_module("app/native")]` function names what TSX may import: components
(`registry.register::<Chart>()`), modules of functions (`registry.module::<Portfolio>()`, `#[module]` on a unit struct and its `impl`),
classes (`registry.class::<Ledger>()`, `#[class]` on a struct and its `impl`) and assets; the attribute also makes
`pub fn registry()` at the crate's root, the same set for your tests and other Rust code (`my_app_native::registry()`,
next to `nsh_base::registry()`). In a `#[module]` or
`#[class]` `impl`, the `pub fn`s are exported (`pub(crate)` too); functions without a visibility are helpers that
stay in Rust. Their TypeScript
declarations, doc comments included, are generated from the Rust types into `.nsh/types`, so TSX is checked against
them by `nsh check` and your editor:

```rust
/// A price chart.
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Props)]
pub struct ChartProps {
    /// The symbol to chart.
    pub symbol: Prop<SharedString>,
    /// The range shown.
    #[prop(default = SharedString::from("1D"))]
    pub range: Prop<SharedString>,
}

#[derive(Event)]
pub enum ChartEvent {
    /// A price was selected.
    #[args(price)]
    Select(f64),
}

/// A price chart; a press selects the last price.
#[component]
pub fn Chart(props: ChartProps, cx: Scope<ChartEvent>) -> impl IntoElement {
    view()
        .h(px(160.0))
        .bg(move || theme().muted)
        .on_press(move || cx.emit(ChartEvent::Select(101.5)))
        .child(text(move || format!("{} · {}", props.symbol.get(), props.range.get())))
}

/// A ledger kept in Rust.
#[class]
pub struct Ledger {
    entries: Vec<f64>,
}

#[class]
impl Ledger {
    /// An empty ledger.
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Ledger { entries: Vec::new() }
    }

    /// Adds `amount`; the new balance.
    pub fn add(&mut self, amount: f64) -> f64 {
        self.entries.push(amount);
        self.balance()
    }

    /// The balance.
    #[getter]
    pub fn balance(&self) -> f64 {
        self.entries.iter().sum()
    }

    /// Uploads the entries; resolves when the server has them.
    pub async fn upload(this: Instance<Ledger>, url: String) -> Result<(), String> {
        let body = this.with(|l| format!("{:?}", l.entries));
        fetch(HttpRequest::post(url, body)).await.map(|_| ())
    }
}

/// The app's holdings.
#[module]
pub struct Portfolio;

#[module]
impl Portfolio {
    /// The value of the holdings.
    pub fn total() -> f64 {
        1250.0
    }
}
```

```tsx
import { mount, signal, View, Text } from "nsh";
import { Chart, Ledger, Portfolio } from "app/native";   // Rust

const ledger = new Ledger();   // its state lives in Rust

function Overview() {
  const balance = signal(ledger.add(Portfolio.total()));   // Rust, called at once
  return (
    <View class="gap-2 p-4">
      <Text>Balance: {balance()}</Text>
      <Chart symbol="NSH" range="1M" onSelect={(e) => balance.set(ledger.add(e.price))} />
      <View onPress={() => ledger.upload("https://example.com/ledger")} role="button" class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 active:bg-blue-700">
        <Text class="text-white">Upload</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(() => <Overview />);
```

Each export is documented in TypeScript by the doc comment of the Rust item that names it: a component by its
`#[component] fn` (`Chart`), a module and a class by their struct (`Portfolio`, `Ledger`), and props, events,
functions and members by their own (a setter needs none beside its getter). The `Props` struct's and the event
enum's own doc comments, and those of `impl` blocks, stay in Rust; a doc comment on a `#[module]` or `#[class]`
`impl` block is a compile error, since TypeScript would not show it. Each command that writes `.nsh/types` warns
about an export TSX sees without a doc comment, naming it (`Ledger.add`, `Chart.range`).

TypeScript shows a doc comment up to its first heading. Notes for Rust callers, such as what `&self` borrows or
why a function takes `cx`, go under a heading, `# Rust` (or rustdoc's `# Panics`, `# Examples`), and stay in the
Rust docs:

```rust
/// Puts `text` on the clipboard; resolves with the number of characters copied.
///
/// # Rust
///
/// Taking `cx` makes it an op, run in order with the UI changes TS made before it.
pub fn copy(text: String, cx: &mut ModuleCx) -> u32 {
    let count = text.chars().count() as u32;
    cx.set_clipboard(text);
    count
}
```

Props are the fields of the component's `Props` struct and events the variants of its `Event` enum (`onSelect`),
both in camel case. Rust code places the same component with its constructor, a setter per prop and a listener
method per event: `chart().symbol("NSH").range("1M").on_select(move |price: &f64| last.set(*price))`. A Rust component's own content, events and state stay in Rust; TSX passes props in and hears
events. A prop of the wrong type (`level={1.5}` for a `u32` prop) is a warning, as on a built-in element: the
prop keeps its value and the rest of the component renders.

A function or a member runs the way its Rust signature says. One that is not `async` runs inside the TSX call and
returns its value (`Portfolio.total()` is a number, `ledger.balance` a property): it computes and keeps state. An
`async fn` returns a Promise and runs as a task with NSH's services (`fetch`, `timer`, dialogs). A module function
taking `cx: &mut ModuleCx` reaches the platform in order with the UI (a toast, the status bar), and so does a
component's ref method; their return type decides what TSX gets: one returning `()` gives `void`, with no reply
(TSX calls it and moves on); one returning `Result<(), E>` gives `Promise<void>`, which rejects with the `Err`'s
message (the call runs with the UI's changes, after the TSX call returned, so the Promise carries its error; one
nobody awaits or catches is logged as an [unhandled rejection](./dev-server-and-debugging.md#logs)); one
returning a value gives `Promise<T>`. Arguments and results are typed from the signature: numbers, strings, `Option`, `Vec`, your
`#[derive(JsObject)]` structs and `#[derive(PropEnum)]` enums, instances of your classes, and TSX functions
(`Callback<A, R>`, which Rust calls at once inside a call, or later with `post` and `call_async`; TS sees
`(value: number) => void` for a `Callback<f64>`, and `#[args(balance)] listener: Callback<f64>` names the argument,
`(balance: number) => void`). A function that starts listening is named `on(event, listener)` and returns `Stop`
(`Stop::new(|| …)`), which TSX gets as a function that stops it (`() => void`); it runs once, when TSX calls it or
when what called `on` goes (a component, or the module's run under hot reload). An event's handler gets one object: a variant's value is its field `value`, which
`#[args(price)]` on the variant names (`onSelect({ price })`), and `#[args(open, reason)]` names the fields of a
variant of several. An argument of
the wrong type throws a `TypeError` in the call, or rejects the Promise of one that returns a Promise; an `Err`
throws (or rejects) with its message. A class's object owns its Rust value: it is freed when the object is collected, or at
once with `ledger.dispose()` (also `using ledger = new Ledger()`). Name the TSX entry to run it, `nsh run App.tsx` or `nsh package App.tsx --target …`: TSX edits are hot
updates, Rust edits rebuild and restart the app. The CLI bundles and compiles the TSX itself, knowing your crate's
exports from its description; the development hosts and `nsh test`'s headless runner are built with your crate and
QuickJS.

`examples/rust-exports` in the repository is the reference for exporting: a small TSX app whose crate exports one
component (props required, defaulted and optional, an event, children), one module (a function of each kind) and
one class (a constructor, methods, a getter and a setter, a static, an `async` member, another instance as an
argument, a callback Rust posts to, `dispose()` and `using`), each with a short doc comment, and tests, in Rust and
in TypeScript (`App.test.tsx`), that press through the app and check what each one shows.

`examples/gallery-rs` in the repository is a complete Rust app: every demo is Rust, `nsh run examples/gallery-rs
--target web` (or `ios`, `android`, …) runs its root, `nsh test examples/gallery-rs` runs its tests headless, and
`cargo run -p gallery-native` starts it on the desktop backend.

### Render functions and the app's classes

A component draws content of the app's for values it has (a row of its data, a code block of a document) with a
render function: a prop `Option<Renderer<T>>`, in TypeScript `(value: T) => JSX.Element`. The component calls
`render(key, value)` where the content goes and gets a view it styles and places as any other (inside a `text(..)`, an
inline view). The content is kept per key while the value stays equal, and rendered again when it changes. A Rust
parent passes a closure to the prop's setter (`quote().render_badge(|symbol| ..)`), which makes the
`Renderer` of it.

Styles in a component are typed; the app's Tailwind classes reach one of its parts through a prop of classes and
`.app_class(..)` on that part's element. They apply after the element's own styles, with the app's theme, `dark:` and
the states, as `class` on an element does.

```rust
/// A quote: its symbol, then content of the app's.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Props)]
pub struct QuoteProps {
    /// The symbol.
    pub symbol: Prop<SharedString>,
    /// Tailwind classes of the symbol's text.
    pub symbol_class: Prop<Option<SharedString>>,
    /// Content of the app's after the symbol (a change, a badge).
    pub render_badge: Prop<Option<Renderer<SharedString>>>,
}

/// A quote of a symbol.
#[component]
pub fn Quote(props: QuoteProps) -> impl IntoElement {
    view()
        .flex_row()
        .items_center()
        .gap_2()
        .child(text(props.symbol).app_class(props.symbol_class))
        .child(dynamic(move || {
            props.render_badge.get().map(|r| r.render("badge", props.symbol.get()).flex_1())
        }))
}
```

```tsx
<Quote
  symbol="NSH"
  symbolClass="text-lg font-semibold"
  renderBadge={(symbol) => <Text class="text-green-600">{`${symbol} ▲ 2.4%`}</Text>}
/>
```

`TextView` in `nsh/base` is built this way: its `renderCodeBlock`, `renderMath`, ... are render functions, and its
`classes` are the app's classes by part ([TextView](../elements/text-view.md)).

## Testing

A Rust app's tests run it headless, in `cargo test` or in `nsh test`, with the same driver: on the real engine,
without a window, with display frames at 60 Hz, so timers, tasks and animations run as on screen. The driver starts
the app, keeps a model of the views it shows and takes steps (`press`, `type_text`, `submit`, `scroll`, `wait_for`)
on views named by selectors (a text, an accessibility label or a test id; `text:`, `label:`, `id:`); a step that
cannot be taken fails with the texts on screen.

In `cargo test`, `nsh_testing::Headless` (nsh-testing's default features, without QuickJS) runs the root
(`app.screen()`: the texts on screen, the commands it sent); `EngineConfig::new` is a phone-sized engine with nothing
else set. `nsh test` runs TypeScript tests ([Testing](./testing-and-trace.md)) in a headless runner built with your
crates, where `open(".")` starts a Rust app's root:

```toml
[dev-dependencies]
nsh-engine = "0.1"
nsh-testing = "0.1"
```

```rust tabs
// tests/app.rs: cargo test
use nsh_engine::{EngineConfig, Root};
use nsh_testing::Headless;

#[test]
fn a_tap_counts() {
    let mut app = Headless::start(EngineConfig::new(Root::of::<my_app::App>())).unwrap();
    app.wait_for("Count: 0").unwrap();
    app.press("Tap").unwrap();
    app.wait_for("Count: 1").unwrap();
}
```

```tsx tabs
// App.test.tsx, next to nsh.json: nsh test
import { expect, open, test } from "nsh/test";

test("a tap counts", async () => {
  const app = await open(".");
  await app.press("Tap");
  expect(app.texts()).toContain("Count: 1");
});
```

A TSX entry is built with `nsh-testing`'s feature `bundle` as `nsh run` builds it, against the UI sets its hosts
serve: NSH's, and each crate's `registry()`, which `#[native_module]` makes:

```toml
[dev-dependencies]
nsh-testing = { version = "0.1", features = ["bundle"] }
nsh-base = "0.1"
```

```rust
#[test]
fn the_module_formats_money() {
    let sets = vec![nsh_base::registry(), my_app_native::registry()];
    let mut app = nsh_testing::tsx("../App.tsx", sets).unwrap();
    app.wait_for("Formatted at once: $1,234.50").unwrap();
}
```

`nsh_testing::compile_tsx` builds the entry once for several tests, and `nsh_testing::start` hands the
batches to a test that keeps its own model of the screen. `examples/rust-exports` tests its TSX entry this way;
`examples/gallery-rs` tests its Rust root in TypeScript, a test file for about each demo.

## Theme

The look of an app is the app's own: NSH provides the primitives and the unstyled base components of `nsh_base`, and
your crate is the styled layer on top, the app's own component library ([Three layers](./architecture.md#three-layers)). Rust components take their colors, corner radius and fonts from a theme, `theme()` from
`nsh_base`, so one file restyles every component of the app. Each color has a light and a dark value;
when the system switches appearance, a binding such as `.bg(move || theme().primary)` changes color natively, with no
render.

The theme has the design tokens of [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/theming), and its default is shadcn's
`neutral` theme, a black-and-white palette with a 10 pt corner radius. To use your own, set `"theme"` in `nsh.json`
to the path of a theme file, relative to `nsh.json`, or to the theme's content inline:

```json
{
  "name": "My App",
  "rust": ".",
  "theme": "brand-theme.json"
}
```

A theme file is shadcn's `cssVars`, the format of shadcn's themes and registry items, so a theme exported from
[shadcn's themes](https://ui.shadcn.com/themes) or [tweakcn](https://tweakcn.com) works as it is. `light` sets the
values of the light appearance, `dark` those of the dark one, and `theme` those of both:

```json
{
  "cssVars": {
    "theme": {
      "radius": "0.5rem",
      "font-sans": "Inter, sans-serif"
    },
    "light": {
      "primary": "oklch(0.541 0.281 293.009)",
      "primary-foreground": "oklch(0.969 0.016 293.756)",
      "ring": "var(--primary)",
      "up": "#16a34a"
    },
    "dark": {
      "primary": "oklch(0.702 0.183 293.541)",
      "primary-foreground": "oklch(0.283 0.141 291.089)",
      "up": "#4ade80"
    }
  }
}
```

- Your theme is applied over the default theme, so you list only what you change. A value `light` sets and `dark`
  leaves out is used in both appearances.
- Values are written as in CSS. Colors are any CSS color (`#7c3aed`, `rgb(…)`, `hsl(…)`, `oklch(…)`, `white`),
  `color-mix(in oklab, var(--primary) 80%, white)`, or another token of the same appearance, `var(--primary)` (with a
  fallback: `var(--brand, #7c3aed)`). Lengths are `rem` (16 points) or `px` (points). Fonts are font family lists:
  the first family that is not a generic one is used, and a generic first family (`system-ui`, `sans-serif`) is the
  system font.
- **Your own tokens.** Any other name is a token of the app, as a variable in Tailwind's `@theme` is: `"up"` above is
  `theme().color("up")` in Rust, `bg-up` / `text-up/70` in classes and `token("up")` in TSX
  ([Theme tokens](./tailwind.md#theme-tokens)). A number such as `"radius-card": "14px"` is `theme().number("radius-card")`
  and `rounded-(--radius-card)`.
- The bundler checks the theme when it builds: a missing file, invalid JSON or a theme other than `cssVars` fails the
  build with an `nsh.json: theme: …` error.

The tokens, with their default light and dark values (shadcn's `neutral`):

| Token | `theme()` | Light | Dark | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `background` / `foreground` | `background` / `foreground` | `oklch(1 0 0)` / `oklch(0.145 0 0)` | `oklch(0.145 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | The app's background, and the text on it |
| `card` / `card-foreground` | `card` / `card_foreground` | `oklch(1 0 0)` / `oklch(0.145 0 0)` | `oklch(0.205 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | Cards and grouped surfaces, and the text on them |
| `popover` / `popover-foreground` | `popover` / `popover_foreground` | `oklch(1 0 0)` / `oklch(0.145 0 0)` | `oklch(0.205 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | Popovers, menus and tooltips, and the text on them |
| `primary` / `primary-foreground` | `primary` / `primary_foreground` | `oklch(0.205 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | `oklch(0.922 0 0)` / `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | The main action (a primary button), and the text on it |
| `secondary` / `secondary-foreground` | `secondary` / `secondary_foreground` | `oklch(0.97 0 0)` / `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | `oklch(0.269 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | Secondary actions, and the text on them |
| `muted` / `muted-foreground` | `muted` / `muted_foreground` | `oklch(0.97 0 0)` / `oklch(0.556 0 0)` | `oklch(0.269 0 0)` / `oklch(0.708 0 0)` | Quiet surfaces; secondary text: captions, labels, placeholders |
| `accent` / `accent-foreground` | `accent` / `accent_foreground` | `oklch(0.97 0 0)` / `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | `oklch(0.269 0 0)` / `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | A hovered or highlighted item, such as a menu item or list row, and its text |
| `destructive` | `destructive` | `oklch(0.577 0.245 27.325)` | `oklch(0.704 0.191 22.216)` | Destructive actions and errors |
| `border` | `border` | `oklch(0.922 0 0)` | `oklch(1 0 0 / 10%)` | Dividers and borders |
| `input` | `input` | `oklch(0.922 0 0)` | `oklch(1 0 0 / 15%)` | The border of inputs |
| `ring` | `ring` | `oklch(0.708 0 0)` | `oklch(0.556 0 0)` | Focus rings |
| `chart-1` … `chart-5` | `chart_1` … `chart_5` | `oklch(0.87 0 0)` … `oklch(0.269 0 0)` | the same | The series of a chart |
| `sidebar`, `sidebar-foreground`, `sidebar-primary`, `sidebar-primary-foreground`, `sidebar-accent`, `sidebar-accent-foreground`, `sidebar-border`, `sidebar-ring` | `sidebar`, `sidebar_foreground`, ... | `sidebar` `oklch(0.985 0 0)`, `sidebar-primary` `oklch(0.205 0 0)` | `sidebar` `oklch(0.205 0 0)`, `sidebar-primary` `oklch(0.488 0.243 264.376)` | A sidebar's surface, its main action, its highlighted item, borders and focus ring |
| `radius` | `radius` | `0.625rem` (10 pt) | | The corner radius |
| `font-sans` | `font_sans` | the system font | | The app's font: every text that sets no family of its own |
| `font-mono` | `font_mono` | the system monospace font | | The monospaced font: `font-mono`, code in `TextView` |

## Several crates

An app's Rust code can be split into crates, each imported by its own specifier: `"rust"` takes a list of crate
paths, and each crate in it has its own `#[native_module]` function.

```json
{
  "rust": ["native/charts", "native/storage"],
  "root": "App"
}
```

```tsx
import { Chart } from "app/charts";        // native/charts: #[native_module("app/charts")]
import { Store } from "app/storage";       // native/storage: #[native_module("app/storage")]
```

Every runner and host links all of them, and `.nsh/types` declares each specifier. Crates share code through Cargo
path dependencies (`shared = { path = "../shared" }`): a crate of company components can be used by several crates
and listed by several apps, and only the crates listed in `"rust"` export to TSX. Each listed crate has a package
name and a specifier of its own; `nsh` reports a repeated one with the two paths that share it. A Rust app's
`"root"` is a component of the first crate listed. During `nsh run` and `nsh dev`, a change to any of them, or to a
crate they depend on by path, rebuilds the app and restarts it.

## Browser APIs on the web

On the web, a crate can call the browser's APIs (a WebSocket, `IndexedDB`, …) through wasm-bindgen and `web-sys`;
`nsh` builds the glue they need with the runtime. See [Web](./web.md#browser-apis-from-rust).
