3:description: Long and endless lists in Rust and TSX - recycling, row identity, columns, sticky headers, inverted chat lists, horizontal lists, lists in a page, loading more, viewability and scrolling to an item.
9:# Lists
11:A list (`virtual_list(..)` in Rust, `List` from `nsh` in TSX) renders long data on a native scroll view while only creating the rows near the screen. Which rows exist, where they go, the columns, sticky headers and which items are visible are all computed natively; your code only fills cells with content when the native side asks for one. A list of a million items costs about as much as a list of thirty.
13:```rust tabs
18:#[component]
55:In Rust, `virtual_list(count, row)` takes the number of rows (a value, a signal or a closure) and a function that builds a row from its position (`at.index()`); the rows read your data by that index. In TSX, `each` takes the items and the row function gets the item. Like a [scroll view](./scrolling.md), the list is the viewport and needs a size from its parent (`.flex_1()`, `flex: 1` or a height).
57:## How recycling works
59:The row function is not called once per item. It is called **once per cell**, and cells are reused: when a row scrolls far off screen, its cell is given another row, and its position (`at.index()` in Rust, `item()` and `index()` in TSX) changes. Everything in the row that reads it updates in place, like any other [signal](./reactivity.md).
65:```rust tabs
92:```rust tabs
138:## Changing the data
140:In Rust, give the count as a signal or a closure (`move || posts.with(Vec::len)`): the list grows and shrinks in place. Rows added or removed at the end need nothing more; when rows come and go elsewhere, give their identities with `.keys(move || posts.with(|p| p.iter().map(|p| p.id).collect::<Vec<_>>()))`, and the list keeps the common start and end and treats what is between as removed and inserted.
152:## Props
154:A list takes every scrolling prop of the scroll view that makes sense for a list (`pagingEnabled`, `snapToInterval`, `snapToOffsets`, `snapToAlignment`, `decelerationRate`, `disableIntervalMomentum`, `bounces`, `scrollable`, `contentInset`, `contentOffset`, `keyboardShouldPersistTaps`, `keyboardDismissMode`, `scrollEventThrottle`, `onScroll`, `onScrollDragStart`, `onScrollDragEnd`, `onMomentumStart`, `onMomentumEnd`, `onScrollEnd`, `scrollValue`, `pullValue`; in Rust the same methods as a scroll view's), described in [Scrolling](./scrolling.md). Lists keep a scale of 1. Its own props:
156:| Prop | Rust | Type | Default | Description |
158:| `each` | `virtual_list(count, ..)` | `readonly T[]` | | The items; in Rust, the number of rows. |
181:| `keyExtractor` | `.keys(..)` | `(item, index) => string` | | The key in viewability tokens; in Rust, the rows' identities. |
189:## Columns and grids
193:```rust tabs
219:## Sticky headers
223:```rust tabs
224:#[derive(Clone, PartialEq)]
282:`stickyHeaderOffset` (`.sticky_header_offset(..)` in Rust) makes the headers stick that many points below the top instead, as CSS `position: sticky`'s `top` does: under a translucent bar 56 points tall, `stickyHeaderOffset={56}` (`.sticky_header_offset(px(56.0))`) keeps each header below the bar while the rows scroll on under it, and the next header pushes it out from there. A negative offset leaves part of a header out of view.
284:The offset can be an [animated value](./animation.md#animated-values) (`.bind_sticky_header_offset(&node)` in Rust): the headers follow it every frame on the UI thread, so they stay below a bar that moves. With a bar that hides as the content scrolls down and comes back as it scrolls up ([`diffClamp`](./animation.md#arithmetic-and-diffclamp)), the headers stick to its bottom edge wherever it is:
286:```rust tabs
310:## Chat: inverted lists
314:```rust tabs
315:#[derive(Clone, PartialEq)]
469:### Following the end of a list that is not inverted
471:A list in reading order (oldest first) can follow its end too: with `.follow_end(px(40.0))` in Rust or `maintainVisibleContentPosition={{ autoscrollToBottomThreshold: 40 }}` in TSX, while the user is at the end (or within 40 points of it), the list stays at the end as the content grows: a reply streaming into the last item, a new message appended, the keyboard shrinking the list. Scrolled further up, the visible content stays where it is and the new content grows below it. Items inserted above the visible ones never move them, with or without the option.
473:```rust tabs

527:## Lists in a page: viewport="parent"
529:A page often scrolls as one: a header, a few cards, then a long list, and maybe another list below it. Give the list `viewport="parent"` (`.viewport(ListViewport::Parent)` in Rust) and put it in a `Scroll` with the rest of the page: the list lies in the page at its full length, and the page's scroll view scrolls it with everything else. It still creates only the rows near the page's viewport and recycles their cells, so one page can hold several long lists.

694:`onViewableItemsChange` (`.on_viewable_items_change(..)`) reports which items are on screen, for analytics, autoplaying the visible video, or marking messages read. In TSX it gets `{ viewableItems, changed }`, arrays of tokens `{ item, key, index, isViewable }`; in Rust, `ViewableItems` with the first and last viewable row (`viewable`) and the rows whose state changed (`changed()`). Viewability is computed natively; your code only hears about changes.

---
title: Carousel
description: "Carousel and its parts: slides shown one place at a time, moved by swiping, the wheel and the touchpad on the platform's own scrolling, by previous and next controls, a pagination and the keyboard, around the ends seamlessly. The carousel owns which slide shows, snapping, looping, the keys and accessibility; the look and every label are the app's."
group: base
demo: el-carousel
---
# Carousel
A carousel shows slides one place at a time: the photos of a product, the steps of an onboarding, a banner that moves
on by itself, a row of cards. `Carousel` owns the behavior: which slide shows, swiping between them, the previous and
next controls, a pagination, the arrow keys, going around the ends, and what screen readers hear. Its parts find it through
context, so the app arranges them freely in its own layout. The look is the app's: no colors, sizes, arrows, dots or
labels of its own.
The content is a native scroll view. A finger, the wheel and the touchpad move the slides on the platform's main
thread, in the same frame as the pointer, and on release the content snaps to the nearest slide, one slide per fling.
When it comes to rest the carousel reports the slide with `onChange`. The controls, the pagination, the keys and the
app's `index` scroll the content natively to the slide, animated.
```rust tabs
use nsh_base::{
    carousel, carousel_content, carousel_item, carousel_next, carousel_pagination,
    carousel_pagination_item, carousel_previous, theme,
};
use nsh_core::prelude::*;
fn photos() -> impl IntoElement {
    let index = signal(0u32);
    let names = ["Harbor", "Dunes", "Glacier"];
    carousel()
        .index(move || Some(index.get()))
        .on_change(move |i: &u32| index.set(*i))
        .accessibility_label("Photos")
        .gap_3()
        .child(
            carousel_content().w_full().h(px(180.0)).gap_3().child(
                names
                    .iter()
                    .enumerate()
                    .map(|(i, name)| {
                        carousel_item()
                            .accessibility_label(format!("{} of 3: {name}", i + 1))
                            .w_full()
                            .rounded(move || theme().radius)
                            .bg(move || theme().muted)
                            .items_center()
                            .justify_center()
                            .child(text(*name))
                    })
                    .collect::<Vec<_>>(),
            ),
        )
        .child(
            view()
                .flex_row()
                .items_center()
                .gap_2()
                .child(carousel_previous().accessibility_label("Previous photo").child(text("‹")))
                .child(
                    carousel_pagination()
                        .flex_row()
                        .gap_1()
                        .child(
                            (0..3)
                                .map(|i| {
                                    carousel_pagination_item()
                                        .index(i)
                                        .accessibility_label(format!("Photo {}", i + 1))
                                        .size_2()
                                        .rounded_full()
                                        .bg(move || theme().border)
                                        .selected_style(|s| s.bg(move || theme().primary))
                                })
                                .collect::<Vec<_>>(),
                        ),
                )
                .child(carousel_next().accessibility_label("Next photo").child(text("›"))),
        )
}
```
```tsx tabs
import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";
import {
  Carousel,
  CarouselContent,
  CarouselItem,
  CarouselNext,
  CarouselPagination,
  CarouselPaginationItem,
  CarouselPrevious,
} from "nsh/base";
const NAMES = ["Harbor", "Dunes", "Glacier"];
function App() {
  const index = signal(0);
  return (
    <Carousel index={index()} onChange={({ index: next }) => index.set(next)} accessibilityLabel="Photos" class="gap-3">
      <CarouselContent class="h-[180px] w-full gap-3">
        {NAMES.map((name, i) => (
          <CarouselItem
            accessibilityLabel={`${i + 1} of ${NAMES.length}: ${name}`}
            class="w-full items-center justify-center rounded-(--radius) bg-muted"
          >
            <Text>{name}</Text>
          </CarouselItem>
        ))}
      </CarouselContent>
      <View class="flex-row items-center gap-2">
        <CarouselPrevious accessibilityLabel="Previous photo" class="disabled:opacity-40">
          <Text>‹</Text>
        </CarouselPrevious>
        <CarouselPagination class="flex-row gap-1">
          {NAMES.map((_, i) => (
            <CarouselPaginationItem
              index={i}
              accessibilityLabel={`Photo ${i + 1}`}
              class="size-2 rounded-full bg-border selected:bg-primary"
            />
          ))}
        </CarouselPagination>
        <CarouselNext accessibilityLabel="Next photo" class="disabled:opacity-40">
          <Text>›</Text>
        </CarouselNext>
      </View>
    </Carousel>
  );
}
mount(App);
```
`Carousel` and its parts come from [`nsh/base`](../modules/nsh-base.md), the `nsh-base` crate in Rust. The slide
shown is the app's `index`: a swipe, a control or a key reports the next one with `onChange`, and the
carousel scrolls to the `index` the app passes back. The slide a swipe rests on shows until the app has answered its
`onChange`: it stays when the app passes it back as `index`, and the content springs back to the app's slide,
animated, when the app keeps the `index` it had. Without `index` the carousel keeps its own, from `defaultIndex`. In Rust,
`carousel()`, `carousel_content()`, `carousel_item()`, `carousel_previous()`, `carousel_next()`,
`carousel_pagination()` and `carousel_pagination_item()` make the parts, with a setter per prop
(`.index(..)`), a listener per event (`.on_change(..)`), the typed style methods and `.child(..)` for their content.
## Props
### Carousel
| Prop | Rust | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `index` | `.index(..)` | `number` | none | The slide shown, from 0, held to the slides there are. The app owns it: changes are reported with `onChange`, and a new `index` scrolls there, animated. |
| `defaultIndex` | `.default_index(..)` | `number` | `0` | The slide shown at first, while `index` is not set. |
| `axis` | `.axis(..)` | `"horizontal" \| "vertical"` | `"horizontal"` | The direction the slides follow each other; read when the carousel is made. A vertical carousel's arrow keys are Up and Down. |
| `looping` | `.looping(..)` | `boolean` | `false` | The slides go around: after the last comes the first, and before the first the last, seamlessly, for a swipe, previous, next, the keys and the app's `index` alike ([Looping](#looping)). Read when the carousel is made. |
| `accessibilityLabel` | `.accessibility_label(..)` | `string` | none | What screen readers call the carousel, a region: what its slides are (`"Featured products"`). |
| `children` | `.child(..)` | `JSX.Element` | none | The `CarouselContent`, the controls and whatever the app lays out around them. |
| `class`, `style` | style methods | `string`, `StyleProp<ViewStyle>` | none | The carousel's layout: where the content and the controls go. |
### CarouselContent
| Prop | Rust | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `.child(..)` | `JSX.Element` | none | The `CarouselItem`s, each a child of the content. |
| `class`, `style` | style methods | `string`, `StyleProp<ViewStyle>` | none | The viewport's size, and the track the slides make in it: a `gap` between them, padding that shows a peek of the slides beside the one in view. |
### CarouselItem
| Prop | Rust | Type | Default | Description |

# The Rust application recipe

The same small app as [the application recipe](tsx-recipe.md), written only in Rust: no TSX and no QuickJS on any
platform. Its files follow the [Coding Guides](coding-guides.md): `src/lib.rs` the root, `src/shell.rs` the stack,
`src/pages/` one file per page, `src/components/` what pages share, `src/store.rs` the state, `src/nav.rs` the routes,
`tests/` the user's flows. This is `examples/tasks-rs` in `longbridge/nsh`, and CI builds and tests that app; there it
inherits its versions from the workspace, while an app of your own starts from `nsh init my-app --template rust`,
whose manifest names them.

What to notice:

- `nsh.json` names the crate (`"rust": "."`) and its root component (`"root": "App"`): `nsh` mounts the root, and
  `src/main.rs` is only for `cargo run`.
- `store.rs` keeps its type and its `tasks()` signal private, so nothing outside can write a task past `add_task`,
  `set_task_done` and `remove_task`. The state is a `global`: one per surface, which also gives each test its own.
- A component runs once. A binding is a closure where a value goes (`text(move || ..)`, `.checked(move || ..)`): it
  reruns when a signal it read changes, and only that prop updates. The store's functions read the signal inside, so
  calling one in a binding tracks it. Listeners read with `get_untracked`: they react to an event, not to a signal.
- `task_detail` gets an `id`, not a `Task`, and reads the task through a closure: it follows the store, and shows
  nothing wrong once the task is gone.
- `task_row` keeps no state, because `virtual_list` makes a cell once and gives it other rows as it recycles: all it
  shows is bound to `at.index()`, and `task_at` answers `None` for a row past the end. `.keys` gives the rows their
  identities, since rows are removed from the middle.
- The draft is a signal of the page that renders it: transient view state stays out of the store. The input is
  controlled, its value given back from the signal.
- Back has two paths that meet in the routes, the only source of truth for the stack. On the desktops and the web the
  page's `header` draws a Back button that calls `nav::pop`. On iOS and Android `title` feeds the system's header; the
  system pops the page itself and `on_dismiss` truncates the routes to match.
- `alert_dialog().show()` returns a future: the listener starts it and awaits it in `spawn`, so nothing blocks while
  the system's alert is up, and the `id` of the chosen action decides (never the label). The page pops before the
  task is removed, so it leaves showing what it showed.
- Colors are `theme()` tokens read in bindings, so they follow the appearance with no render. The switch's parts take
  classes, since `checked:` has to follow the switch's state.
- The tests take a user's steps on the real engine, headless: `on_dialog` answers the alert, first with Cancel to show
  that only Remove removes, and `back` goes back as the platform does.

# Everbloom

An app written in Rust: its UI is `src/lib.rs`, and `nsh.json` names the root component (`"root": "App"`).

```sh
nsh run                      # this machine's backend; --target ios, android, web, macos, linux or windows
nsh check                    # cargo check of the crate, then type checks App.test.tsx
nsh test                     # cargo test, then App.test.tsx: the root tested from TypeScript, headless; --target to run it on a platform
nsh test nsh.json --trace    # headless: what the root mounts, and the time of each commit
nsh package --target web     # or ios, android, macos, linux, windows
```

`nsh run` and `nsh package` mount the root on every platform, the browser included, without QuickJS: the app is Rust
and native code from start to end (in the browser, with NSH's page script). Rust edits rebuild and restart the app.

```sh
cargo run
```

This starts the root directly on the machine's native desktop backend: GTK 4 on Linux, AppKit on macOS, Win32 on
Windows. Install the backend's development libraries before building.

The `nsh` commands build the app's runners from the NSH crates `Cargo.toml` depends on: crates.io's at the version of
the `nsh` you run (keep the `nsh-*` dependencies at that version when you upgrade `nsh`), or an NSH checkout's by path.

## Adding a TSX entry

TSX screens can use the Rust components and modules, with hot reloading for the TSX. The crate's set,
`#[native_module("everbloom/native")]` in `src/lib.rs`, already exports `App`. Add an `App.tsx`:

```tsx
import { mount } from "nsh";
import { App } from "everbloom/native";

mount(App);
```

then run it with `nsh run App.tsx` (`tsconfig.json` is there for it and the test): a named TSX entry
runs on QuickJS, while `nsh run` alone keeps running the Rust root. The first `nsh build App.tsx` writes the TypeScript
declarations of `everbloom/native` into `.nsh/types`. Register more with `registry.register::<…>()` (components),
`registry.module::<…>()` and `registry.class::<…>()`.

NSH-generated files stay in `.nsh/`: runner sources in `.nsh/rust/` and default packages in `.nsh/out/`.
Cargo keeps its normal `target/` directory and respects your existing `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`.

content.content:
---
title: Progress
description: "The Progress component: a linear progress bar that owns its role, range and value for screen readers and the indicator's width by the value, with a track and an indicator the app styles."
group: base
demo: el-progress
---
# Progress
A progress bar shows how far a task with a known extent is (a download, an upload, a step of a setup), or, while
`indeterminate`, that a task of unknown extent is under way. It owns what screen readers get, the progress bar role
with the range 0 to 100 and the value, and the indicator's width: `value` percent of the track's. The look is the
app's: a `Progress` has no colors, sizes, radii, motion or label of its own. It is made of a track with an indicator
inside it, then its children (a label, the value as text), and the app styles each part.
```rust tabs
use nsh_base::{progress, theme};
use nsh_core::prelude::*;
fn upload(sent: Signal<f32>) -> impl IntoElement {
    progress()
        .value(sent)
        .accessibility_label("Uploading photos")
        .gap_2()
        .track_style(|s| s.h(px(8.0)).rounded_full().overflow_hidden().bg(move || theme().muted))
        .indicator_style(|s| s.h_full().rounded_full().bg(move || theme().primary))
        .child(
            text(move || format!("{:.0}%", sent.get()))
                .text_sm()
                .text_color(move || theme().muted_foreground),
        )
}
```
```tsx tabs
import { mount, signal, Text } from "nsh";
import { Progress } from "nsh/base";
function App() {
  const sent = signal(40);
  return (
    <Progress
      value={sent()}
      accessibilityLabel="Uploading photos"
      class="gap-2"
      trackClass="h-2 overflow-hidden rounded-full bg-muted"
      indicatorClass="h-full rounded-full bg-primary"
    >
      <Text class="text-sm text-muted-foreground">{`${sent()}%`}</Text>
    </Progress>
  );
}
mount(App);
```
`Progress` comes from [`nsh/base`](../modules/nsh-base.md), the `nsh-base` crate in Rust. The value is the app's: the
progress bar shows the `value` the app passes, held to 0 to 100. In Rust, `progress()` makes one with a setter per prop

cd /Users/itome/shopbench-runs/nsh/ios && cat > build-rust.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# Xcode's "Build Rust" phase: builds the app's Rust half (ios/rust) as a
# static library for the SDK being built, in release mode, into
# ios/rust/target/<rust target>/release/libeverbloom_ios.a.
set -eu

case "${PLATFORM_NAME:-iphonesimulator}" in
  iphoneos) TARGET=aarch64-apple-ios ;;
  iphonesimulator) TARGET=aarch64-apple-ios-sim ;;
  *) echo "error: unsupported platform ${PLATFORM_NAME}" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
CARGO_BIN="${CARGO_HOME:-$HOME/.cargo}/bin"

# A clean environment: Xcode's SDKROOT and friends would point the host
# build scripts at the iOS SDK.
exec env -i \
  HOME="$HOME" \
  PATH="$CARGO_BIN:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin" \
  ${RUSTUP_HOME:+RUSTUP_HOME="$RUSTUP_HOME"} \
  ${CARGO_HOME:+CARGO_HOME="$CARGO_HOME"} \
  IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET="${IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET:-15.0}" \

content.text: Scrolls to the end once the keyboard is dismissed. Checking whether scrolling with the keyboard still up actually fails (the benchmark may do exactly that).

input.command:
cat >> ios/EverbloomUITests/FlowTests.swift <<'EOF'

final class KeyboardScrollTests: XCTestCase {
    func testResultsScrollWithKeyboardUp() {
        let app = XCUIApplication()
        app.launch()
        let any = app.descendants(matching: .any)
        any.matching(identifier: "tab-search").firstMatch.tap()
        let field = any.matching(identifier: "search-input").firstMatch
        XCTAssertTrue(field.waitForExistence(timeout: 10))
        field.tap()
        field.typeText("shirt")
        let results = any.matching(identifier: "search-results").firstMatch
        XCTAssertTrue(any.matching(identifier: "search-result-0").firstMatch.waitForExistence(timeout: 20))
        print("=== keyboard up: \(app.keyboards.count)")
        results.swipeUp()
        sleep(1)
        print("=== keyboard after swipe: \(app.keyboards.count)")
        results.swipeUp()
        results.swipeUp()
        sleep(1)
        let rows = any.matching(NSPredicate(format: "identifier BEGINSWITH 'search-result-'"))
            .allElementsBoundByIndex.filter { $0.isHittable }.map(\.identifier)
        print("=== hittable rows \(rows)")
        let shot = XCTAttachment(screenshot: app.screenshot())
        shot.lifetime = .keepAlways
        add(shot)
        XCTAssertFalse(rows.contains("search-result-0"))
    }
}
EOF

        shot("1-home")

        shot("3-collection")
        el("sort-price-desc").tap()
        XCTAssertTrue(el("product-card-0").waitForExistence(timeout: 20))
        shot("4-collection-sorted")
        el("product-card-0").tap()
        XCTAssertTrue(el("add-to-cart").waitForExistence(timeout: 20))
        shot("5-product")

        shot("6-product-scrolled")

        shot("7-cart")

        el("search-input").typeText("linen")

        el("qty-dec-0").tap()

    }
}

detail: Android APK built; adding cleartext manifest post-process

content.text: Writing `android/package.sh`: runs `nsh package`, then relinks the manifest (cleartext HTTP, portrait), realigns and re-signs with the debug key.

input.command:
mkdir -p /Users/itome/shopbench-runs/nsh/android && cd /Users/itome/shopbench-runs/nsh/android && cat > AndroidManifest.xml <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<!-- The manifest `nsh package --target android` writes for a Rust app, plus
     cleartext HTTP (the benchmark's replay server on the local network) and
     portrait only. android/package.sh links it into the APK. -->
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android" package="dev.whiskerrs.shopbench.nsh">
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
    <application android:label="Everbloom"
        android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"
        android:extractNativeLibs="false"
        android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true"
        android:supportsRtl="true"
        android:theme="@android:style/Theme.Material.Light.NoActionBar">
        <meta-data android:name="com.longbridge.nsh.RUST" android:value="true" />
        <activity android:name="com.longbridge.nsh.AppActivity" android:exported="true"
            android:screenOrientation="portrait"
            android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize"
            android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize|screenLayout|smallestScreenSize|keyboard|keyboardHidden|navigation|uiMode|density|fontScale|locale|layoutDirection">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>
    </application>
</manifest>
EOF
cat > package.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# Builds the Android release APK: `nsh package --target android` (release
# runtime, the app's Rust root in libnsh.so), then links the APK again with
# android/AndroidManifest.xml (cleartext HTTP, portrait), aligns it and signs
# it with the debug key. Writes build/android/Everbloom.apk.
#
# SHOP_API_URL, when set, is compiled in as the API endpoint.
set -eu

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
SDK="${ANDROID_HOME:-${ANDROID_SDK_ROOT:-$HOME/Library/Android/sdk}}"
BT="$(ls -d "$SDK"/build-tools/* | sort -V | tail -1)"
JAR="$SDK/platforms/android-35/android.jar"
OUT="$ROOT/build/android"
WORK="$OUT/work"

cd "$ROOT"
nsh package --target android --out "$OUT/nsh"

rm -rf "$WORK" && mkdir -p "$WORK/files"
"$BT/aapt2" link -o "$WORK/base.apk" -I "$JAR" \
  --manifest "$ROOT/android/AndroidManifest.xml" \
  --min-sdk-version 28 --target-sdk-version 35 \
  --version-code 1 --version-name 1.0.0

# Code, native libraries (stored, page aligned) and assets from nsh's APK.
(cd "$WORK/files" && unzip -q "$OUT/nsh/Everbloom.apk" 'classes.dex' 'lib/*' 'assets/*')
cp "$WORK/base.apk" "$WORK/unaligned.apk"
(cd "$WORK/files" && zip -q -X "$WORK/unaligned.apk" classes.dex && zip -q -X -r "$WORK/unaligned.apk" assets && zip -q -X -0 -r "$WORK/unaligned.apk" lib)
"$BT/zipalign" -P 16 -f 4 "$WORK/unaligned.apk" "$WORK/aligned.apk"

KEYSTORE="$HOME/.android/debug.keystore"
if [ ! -f "$KEYSTORE" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$HOME/.android"
  keytool -genkeypair -keystore "$KEYSTORE" -storepass android -keypass android \
    -alias androiddebugkey -dname "CN=Android Debug,O=Android,C=US" \
    -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
fi
"$BT/apksigner" sign --ks "$KEYSTORE" --ks-pass pass:android --key-pass pass:android \
  --ks-key-alias androiddebugkey --out "$OUT/Everbloom.apk" "$WORK/aligned.apk"
rm -rf "$WORK"
echo "built $OUT/Everbloom.apk"
EOF
chmod +x package.sh && cd .. && time ./android/package.sh 2>&1 | tail -4 && ~/Library/Android/sdk/build-tools/36.0.0/aapt2 dump xmltree --file AndroidManifest.xml build/android/Everbloom.apk | grep -i "cleartext\|screenOrientation"

#!/bin/sh
# Builds the Android release APK: `nsh package --target android` (release
# runtime, the app's Rust root in libnsh.so), then links the APK again with
# android/AndroidManifest.xml (cleartext HTTP, portrait), aligns it and signs
# it with the debug key. Writes build/android/Everbloom.apk.
#
# SHOP_API_URL, when set, is compiled in as the API endpoint.
set -eu

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
SDK="${ANDROID_HOME:-${ANDROID_SDK_ROOT:-$HOME/Library/Android/sdk}}"
BT="$(ls -d "$SDK"/build-tools/* | sort -V | tail -1)"
JAR="$SDK/platforms/android-35/android.jar"
OUT="$ROOT/build/android"
WORK="$OUT/work"

cd "$ROOT"
nsh package --target android --out "$OUT/nsh"

rm -rf "$WORK" && mkdir -p "$WORK/files"
"$BT/aapt2" link -o "$WORK/base.apk" -I "$JAR" \
  --manifest "$ROOT/android/AndroidManifest.xml" \
  --min-sdk-version 28 --target-sdk-version 35 \
  --version-code 1 --version-name 1.0.0

# Code, native libraries (stored, page aligned) and assets from nsh's APK.
(cd "$WORK/files" && unzip -q "$OUT/nsh/Everbloom.apk" 'classes.dex' 'lib/*' 'assets/*')
cp "$WORK/base.apk" "$WORK/unaligned.apk"
(cd "$WORK/files" && zip -q -X "$WORK/unaligned.apk" classes.dex && zip -q -X -r "$WORK/unaligned.apk" assets && zip -q -X -0 -r "$WORK/unaligned.apk" lib)
"$BT/zipalign" -P 16 -f 4 "$WORK/unaligned.apk" "$WORK/aligned.apk"

KEYSTORE="$HOME/.android/debug.keystore"
if [ ! -f "$KEYSTORE" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$HOME/.android"
  keytool -genkeypair -keystore "$KEYSTORE" -storepass android -keypass android \
    -alias androiddebugkey -dname "CN=Android Debug,O=Android,C=US" \
    -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
fi
"$BT/apksigner" sign --ks "$KEYSTORE" --ks-pass pass:android --key-pass pass:android \
  --ks-key-alias androiddebugkey --out "$OUT/Everbloom.apk" "$WORK/aligned.apk"
rm -rf "$WORK"
echo "built $OUT/Everbloom.apk"
EOF

final class KeyboardScrollTests: XCTestCase {
    func testResultsScrollWithKeyboardUp() {
        let app = XCUIApplication()
        app.launch()
        let any = app.descendants(matching: .any)
        any.matching(identifier: "tab-search").firstMatch.tap()
        let field = any.matching(identifier: "search-input").firstMatch
        XCTAssertTrue(field.waitForExistence(timeout: 10))
        field.tap()
        field.typeText("shirt")
        let results = any.matching(identifier: "search-results").firstMatch
        XCTAssertTrue(any.matching(identifier: "search-result-0").firstMatch.waitForExistence(timeout: 20))
        print("=== keyboard up: \(app.keyboards.count)")
        results.swipeUp()
        sleep(1)
        print("=== keyboard after swipe: \(app.keyboards.count)")

        sleep(1)
        let rows = any.matching(NSPredicate(format: "identifier BEGINSWITH 'search-result-'"))
            .allElementsBoundByIndex.filter { $0.isHittable }.map(\.identifier)
        print("=== hittable rows \(rows)")
        let shot = XCTAttachment(screenshot: app.screenshot())
        shot.lifetime = .keepAlways
        add(shot)
        XCTAssertFalse(rows.contains("search-result-0"))
        any.matching(identifier: rows[1]).firstMatch.tap()
        XCTAssertTrue(any.matching(identifier: "add-to-cart").firstMatch.waitForExistence(timeout: 15))
    }
}

# Building Everbloom

Run every command from the project root. Outputs go to `build/` (and Cargo's `target/`, `ios/rust/target/`).

## 1. Install dependencies

Required: macOS with Xcode 26 (iOS SDK and an iOS simulator runtime), Homebrew, rustup, and for Android the Android
SDK with platform 35, build-tools and an NDK.

```sh
# Native Shell's CLI, 0.4.0 (the app's NSH crates are pinned to the same version)
brew install longbridge/tap/nsh

# Rust 1.98.1 with the iOS and Android targets (rust-toolchain.toml selects it)
rustup toolchain install 1.98.1 --profile minimal \
  --target aarch64-apple-ios aarch64-apple-ios-sim aarch64-linux-android armv7-linux-androideabi x86_64-linux-android

# Rust crates (NSH comes from its Git tag v0.4.0)
cargo fetch --locked
cargo fetch --locked --manifest-path ios/rust/Cargo.toml

# Android SDK parts (ANDROID_HOME defaults to ~/Library/Android/sdk)
"${ANDROID_HOME:-$HOME/Library/Android/sdk}/cmdline-tools/latest/bin/sdkmanager" \
  "platforms;android-35" "build-tools;36.0.0" "ndk;29.0.14206865" "platform-tools"
```

`ios/Everbloom.xcodeproj` is committed; it was generated from `ios/project.yml` with xcodegen, which is only needed to
regenerate it (`cd ios && xcodegen generate`).

## 2. iOS device release build (benchmarked)

Signed, with automatic signing for the team in `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM`:

```sh
export DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=ABCDE12345   # your Apple team ID
xcodebuild -project ios/Everbloom.xcodeproj -scheme Everbloom -configuration Release \
  -sdk iphoneos -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' -derivedDataPath build/ios-device \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates DEVELOPMENT_TEAM="$DEVELOPMENT_TEAM" build
```

Without a team (signing disabled):

```sh
xcodebuild -project ios/Everbloom.xcodeproj -scheme Everbloom -configuration Release \
  -sdk iphoneos -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' -derivedDataPath build/ios-device \
  CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO build
```

The app: `build/ios-device/Build/Products/Release-iphoneos/Everbloom.app`

The Xcode target's "Build Rust" phase (`ios/build-rust.sh`) builds the Rust half with
`cargo build --release --target aarch64-apple-ios` (fat LTO, one codegen unit) before Xcode links it. The first build
compiles NSH and takes a few minutes.

## 3. Install and launch on a connected iPhone

```sh
xcrun devicectl list devices                      # note the device's identifier
DEVICE=<device identifier>
xcrun devicectl device install app --device "$DEVICE" \
  build/ios-device/Build/Products/Release-iphoneos/Everbloom.app
xcrun devicectl device process launch --device "$DEVICE" --terminate-existing \
  --environment-variables '{"SHOP_API_URL":"http://192.168.1.20:8787/api"}' \
  dev.whiskerrs.shopbench.nsh
```

Leave out `--environment-variables` (or pass an empty value) to use `https://apparel-large-catalog.mock.shop/api`.
The app writes `SHOPBENCH home_ready` with `os_log` once Home shows its content (Console.app, the device's log).

## 4. iOS Simulator build (verification)

Same project, Release configuration, simulator SDK (arm64):

```sh
xcodebuild -project ios/Everbloom.xcodeproj -scheme Everbloom -configuration Release \
  -sdk iphonesimulator -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator' -derivedDataPath build/ios-sim build
```

The app: `build/ios-sim/Build/Products/Release-iphonesimulator/Everbloom.app`

```sh
xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 17 Pro" 2>/dev/null || true    # or any booted simulator
xcrun simctl install booted build/ios-sim/Build/Products/Release-iphonesimulator/Everbloom.app
SIMCTL_CHILD_SHOP_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787/api xcrun simctl launch --terminate-running-process booted dev.whiskerrs.shopbench.nsh
# the log marker:
xcrun simctl spawn booted log stream --style compact --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS "SHOPBENCH"'
```

Without `SIMCTL_CHILD_SHOP_API_URL` the app uses mock.shop.

Optional, the UI tests used during development (flows, identifiers, error and Retry, keyboard scrolling):

```sh
xcodebuild test -project ios/Everbloom.xcodeproj -scheme Everbloom \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' -derivedDataPath build/ios-test \
  -skip-testing:EverbloomUITests/ErrorStateTests
```

(`ErrorStateTests` expects a server to start on `127.0.0.1:8787` while the error shows.)

## 5. Android release APK

```sh
./android/package.sh
```

The APK: `build/android/Everbloom.apk` (arm64-v8a and armeabi-v7a, signed with the debug key).

The endpoint is a build-time setting: set `SHOP_API_URL` while building, for example

```sh
SHOP_API_URL=http://192.168.1.20:8787/api ./android/package.sh
SHOP_API_URL=http://10.0.2.2:8787/api ./android/package.sh      # the host machine, from the emulator
```

Unset or empty, the app uses mock.shop. Install and launch:

```sh
adb install -r build/android/Everbloom.apk
adb shell am start -n dev.whiskerrs.shopbench.nsh/com.longbridge.nsh.AppActivity
```

`android/package.sh` runs `nsh package --target android` (NSH's release runtime with the app's Rust root in
`libnsh.so`), then links the APK again with `android/AndroidManifest.xml`, NSH's manifest plus cleartext HTTP and
portrait orientation, aligns it (16 KB pages) and signs it.

## 6. Build modes and toolchain

| Build | Mode |
|---|---|
| iOS device | Xcode Release configuration (`-Os` for `main.m`, stripped, dead-code stripped); Rust `--release` with fat LTO, `codegen-units = 1`, `opt-level = 3`; NSH's Rust backend without QuickJS, no dev server, no hot reload, no debug overlay |
| iOS Simulator | The same Release configuration and Rust release profile, for `aarch64-apple-ios-sim`: the most production-like mode, identical to the device build but for the target |
| Android | `nsh package --target android`: NSH's release runtime (`AppActivity`, no dev server), the Rust crate in release mode; debug-key signed |

Versions used:

- macOS 26.5.1, Xcode 26.6 (iOS SDK 26.5), iOS Simulator runtime 26.5 (iPhone 17 Pro)
- Native Shell 0.4.0 (CLI `nsh 0.4.0 (e626a8d)`, crates from `https://github.com/longbridge/nsh` tag `v0.4.0`)
- Rust 1.98.1 (`rust-toolchain.toml`)
- Android SDK platform 35, build-tools 37.0.0, NDK 29.0.14206865, emulator 37.1.11 with an Android 37.1 arm64 image;
  OpenJDK 21 (`keytool`)
- xcodegen 2.45.4 (only to regenerate the Xcode project)

# Notes

## How the app is built

- **Rust, no TSX.** The whole app is a Rust crate (`src/`) on Native Shell's engine; `nsh.json` names its root
  component (`App`). No JavaScript VM ships in either app.
- **NSH from its Git tag.** The app depends on NSH 0.4.0 from `https://github.com/longbridge/nsh` tag `v0.4.0`, not
  crates.io: the crates.io package of `nsh-platform-ios` 0.4.0 does not compile (its `lib.rs` includes
  `../../nsh-platform-macos/src/speech.rs`, a file outside the published crate). The Git checkout is the same release.
  NSH itself is not modified.
- **iOS: an Xcode project around a Rust static library.** `ios/rust` is a `staticlib` crate whose
  `everbloom_main()` calls `nsh_platform_ios::run_app` with the app's root (what `nsh package` does in its own
  runner); `ios/Everbloom/main.m` calls it. I used this instead of `nsh package --target ios` because the spec needs
  things `nsh package` cannot set: App Transport Security for plain HTTP, portrait only, iPhone only, automatic
  signing from `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` / `CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO`, and an `os_log` call for the log marker.
  The project was generated by xcodegen from `ios/project.yml` and is committed, so building needs no xcodegen.
- **Android: `nsh package` plus a manifest.** NSH's release manifest has no cleartext HTTP setting (it adds
  `usesCleartextTraffic` only to development builds) and allows every orientation. `android/package.sh` keeps NSH's APK
  contents (`classes.dex`, `libnsh.so`, assets) and links them with `android/AndroidManifest.xml`: NSH's manifest plus
  `usesCleartextTraffic="true"` and `screenOrientation="portrait"`.
- **Endpoint.** iOS reads `SHOP_API_URL` from the process environment at launch. Android uses `SHOP_API_URL` from the
  build environment (compiled in with `option_env!`; `build.rs` rebuilds when it changes). The iOS build script runs
  Cargo with a clean environment, so a `SHOP_API_URL` in the shell is never compiled into the iOS app.
- **Log marker.** `SHOPBENCH home_ready` is written with `os_log(OS_LOG_DEFAULT, …)` from `main.m`, once per process,
  on the frame after Home's data is set. Nothing else is logged by the app (NSH's runner logs nothing in release).

## Decisions where the spec is silent

- **Tab bar.** A custom bar drawn from the design (49 pt + safe area, the design's SVG icons, the badge). NSH's
  system `TabBar` uses SF Symbols / drawables and has no badge or test ids. Tabs are kept mounted and hidden, so each
  keeps its stack. The bar is hidden when the selected tab shows a product, and while the software keyboard is up
  (the content is padded above the keyboard, so the search results end at its top instead of under it).
- **Navigation.** Each of Home and Search is an NSH `nav_stack` (native `UINavigationController` / Android stack,
  native push animation and swipe back) with the system header hidden; pages draw the design's own bars. Collection
  and Search show the tab bar; Product hides it.
- **Collection screen.** The title comes from the collection tapped on Home (shown at once); the description and the
  sort chips sit above the grid, which is the scrolling container (`product-grid`). A sort change clears the grid and
  shows the skeleton until the first page of the new order arrives; answers to an older sort are dropped.
- **Infinite scroll** uses NSH's `virtual_list` `on_load_more` with its default threshold of one viewport. The
  "small loading indicator" is the text "Loading…" in `textMuted` at the end of the list (NSH has no activity
  indicator control and the spec allows no extra animation). A failed next page stops loading until the next scroll
  to the end.
- **Lazy rendering.** Collection grid and search results are `virtual_list`s (native recycling). Because test ids in
  NSH's Rust API are static, each cell rebuilds its card when it is given another row (`dynamic` over the row
  index), so `product-card-<i>` / `search-result-<i>` always name the row shown.
- **Pressables** are NSH views in the `button` role with `on_press` (NSH 0.4.0's Rust component builder has no
  `test_id`, while views do, and a pressable view is one accessibility element carrying its identifier).
  `product-carousel` is set on a group view around NSH's `carousel` (its parts take no test id).
- **Product.** The carousel is NSH's `carousel` (native paging scroll view) with page dots (only with 2+ images) and
  the round back button over it. The price uses the `sale` color with the compare-at price struck through when the
  compare-at is higher (as on cards). Option label is `<name>: <value>` with the value in `textMuted`. When no variant
  matches the combination exactly, the first variant with the tapped value is selected. Sections without data
  (description, recommendations) are left out.
- **Prices:** search rows and recommendation cards show the price only (as drawn); grid cards and best sellers show
  the sale treatment.
- **Featured banner** label is "Featured collection" drawn uppercase (the design's `text-transform`).
- **"See all"** next to "Collections" in the design is left out: the spec lists no such feature.
- **Empty cart** "Start shopping" (from the design's empty state) switches to the Home tab.
- **Search.** The text is trimmed before sending; an empty field shows the hint and no results. A new query replaces
  the results with skeleton rows once it is sent (after the 300 ms pause). Stale answers are dropped by a generation
  counter. Taps on a result work while the keyboard is up; dragging the list dismisses the keyboard.
- **Cart.** Steppers are disabled while a cart mutation is in flight (so quick taps cannot send stale quantities).
  "Add to cart" switches to the Cart tab once the server answered; a network failure of any cart mutation shows the
  alert "Couldn't update the cart. Check your connection and try again." (the spec only defines the `userErrors`
  alert, which shows the first message). The variant title line is omitted for `Default Title`.
- **Check out** opens `checkoutUrl` in the system browser (`open_url`): NSH has no in-app browser.
- **Loading states.** Home: the skeleton of `States.dc.html`, from the first frame. Collection: a skeleton grid.
  Product: a skeleton image and title with the back button. Search: skeleton rows. Error copy uses the spec's
  "Couldn't load products" (ASCII apostrophe).
- **Images** are requested with `width` exactly as the table says (1080 banner/carousel, 480 cards, 240 thumbnails
  and cart lines) and drawn aspect-fill on the `surface` color.
- **Launch screen** is the system's plain launch screen (`UILaunchScreen` empty, light appearance): white.
- **Debug key** signs the Android APK.

## Dependencies added

- `serde` (with `derive`): decoding the Storefront API's JSON into typed models.
- `serde_json`: building request bodies and parsing responses.

Nothing else: no UI kit, state library or GraphQL client. Requests are plain `POST`s through NSH's `fetch`
(NSURLSession on iOS, HttpURLConnection on Android). xcodegen was used once to generate the Xcode project; it is not
needed to build.

## Not met, or met with caveats

- **In-app browser:** NSH has none, so Check out opens the system browser (the spec's stated fallback).
- **Signed iOS build** could not be run here: this machine's Xcode account login is rejected, so automatic
  provisioning fails. The unsigned device build (`CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO`) and the simulator build succeed; the
  signed command is standard automatic signing.
- **Loading indicator** at the end of lists is a text, not a spinner (see above).
- **Accessibility labels of containers.** NSH reads the text inside a view as the label of a container without one,
  including the text of hidden tabs, so some "Other" elements in XCUITest carry long labels. Identifiers are
  unaffected; elements in hidden tabs are not exposed.
- **Android endpoint** is set at build time (allowed by the spec), not at launch.

content.text:
The Everbloom app is built with Native Shell 0.4.0, written entirely in Rust. Every item on the spec's done checklist passes except one I couldn't test here: the signed iOS device build.

**Verified**
- **BUILD.md from a clean copy:** the unsigned iOS device build, the simulator build and the Android release APK all succeed. Both iOS builds use the Release configuration.
- **iOS Simulator, via UI tests I added (`ios/EverbloomUITests`):**
  - Home loads with all its identifiers.
  - A collection scrolls through 84 products across several pages, and each sort reloads it.
  - Search returns results and scrolls to the end (67 results for "shirt").
  - On a product, the option pills switch the variant and recommendations open another product. No product in the first 100 best sellers has different prices per variant, so I couldn't see the price itself change; it follows the selected variant.
  - Add to cart switches to Cart with badge "1"; the steppers change quantity and subtotal; going to 0 shows the empty state.
  - Check out opens Safari.
  - With the endpoint unreachable, Home shows the error state, and Retry works once a local plain-HTTP server comes up.
- **Log marker:** `SHOPBENCH home_ready` appears exactly once per launch.
- **Android emulator:** Home loads, and a build-time `SHOP_API_URL` over plain HTTP reaches a local server. The emulator's DNS failed at first; restarting it with `-dns-server` fixed that, and the app wasn't at fault.

**Not verified:** the signed build with `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM`. This Mac's Xcode account login is rejected, so automatic provisioning fails here. The command in BUILD.md is the standard one.

**Things that differ from a stock NSH setup**
- **NSH comes from its GitHub tag `v0.4.0`, not crates.io.** The published `nsh-platform-ios 0.4.0` doesn't compile because it includes a file outside the crate. The Git tag is the same release, unmodified.
- **iOS uses my own Xcode project instead of `nsh package`.** It wraps the Rust code as a static library and starts NSH's own UIKit runner. `nsh package` can't set what the spec needs: plain HTTP (App Transport Security), portrait only, `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` signing, and the `os_log` marker. The release binary is 27 MB, against 44 MB from `nsh package`.
- **Android uses `nsh package`, then `android/package.sh` re-links the manifest** to allow plain HTTP and lock portrait. NSH only allows plain HTTP in development builds.
- **Check out opens the system browser**, because NSH has no in-app browser (the spec's stated fallback).
- **The end-of-list loading indicator is the text "Loading…"**, because NSH has no spinner control.
- **The tab bar hides while the keyboard is up.** The search results then end at the keyboard's top, and a tap on a result works without first dismissing the keyboard. Without this, swiping the results with the keyboard up didn't scroll in the UI tests.

Everything else I decided where the spec was silent is in `NOTES.md`, and build commands and toolchain versions are in `BUILD.md`.

status_detail: shop app built for iOS and Android; signed iOS build unverified

result:
The Everbloom app is built with Native Shell 0.4.0, written entirely in Rust. Every item on the spec's done checklist passes except one I couldn't test here: the signed iOS device build.

**Verified**
- **BUILD.md from a clean copy:** the unsigned iOS device build, the simulator build and the Android release APK all succeed. Both iOS builds use the Release configuration.
- **iOS Simulator, via UI tests I added (`ios/EverbloomUITests`):**
  - Home loads with all its identifiers.
  - A collection scrolls through 84 products across several pages, and each sort reloads it.
  - Search returns results and scrolls to the end (67 results for "shirt").
  - On a product, the option pills switch the variant and recommendations open another product. No product in the first 100 best sellers has different prices per variant, so I couldn't see the price itself change; it follows the selected variant.
  - Add to cart switches to Cart with badge "1"; the steppers change quantity and subtotal; going to 0 shows the empty state.
  - Check out opens Safari.
  - With the endpoint unreachable, Home shows the error state, and Retry works once a local plain-HTTP server comes up.
- **Log marker:** `SHOPBENCH home_ready` appears exactly once per launch.
- **Android emulator:** Home loads, and a build-time `SHOP_API_URL` over plain HTTP reaches a local server. The emulator's DNS failed at first; restarting it with `-dns-server` fixed that, and the app wasn't at fault.

**Not verified:** the signed build with `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM`. This Mac's Xcode account login is rejected, so automatic provisioning fails here. The command in BUILD.md is the standard one.

**Things that differ from a stock NSH setup**
- **NSH comes from its GitHub tag `v0.4.0`, not crates.io.** The published `nsh-platform-ios 0.4.0` doesn't compile because it includes a file outside the crate. The Git tag is the same release, unmodified.
- **iOS uses my own Xcode project instead of `nsh package`.** It wraps the Rust code as a static library and starts NSH's own UIKit runner. `nsh package` can't set what the spec needs: plain HTTP (App Transport Security), portrait only, `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` signing, and the `os_log` marker. The release binary is 27 MB, against 44 MB from `nsh package`.
- **Android uses `nsh package`, then `android/package.sh` re-links the manifest** to allow plain HTTP and lock portrait. NSH only allows plain HTTP in development builds.
- **Check out opens the system browser**, because NSH has no in-app browser (the spec's stated fallback).
- **The end-of-list loading indicator is the text "Loading…"**, because NSH has no spinner control.
- **The tab bar hides while the keyboard is up.** The search results then end at the keyboard's top, and a tap on a result works without first dismissing the keyboard. Without this, swiping the results with the keyboard up didn't scroll in the UI tests.
- **Dependencies added:** only `serde` and `serde_json`.

Everything else I decided where the spec was silent is in `NOTES.md`, and build commands and toolchain versions are in `BUILD.md`.
